We have said: (Ḥā Mīm) is one of the disjoined letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa). Scholars have circled around the meanings of these letters, and these attempts are meant to satisfy the craving of the mind for inquiry. But faith is otherwise. Faith takes the matter as a given (musallama), and since God has said it, the question is settled.

This is why, when they said to our master Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, "Your companion claims that he did such-and-such," he said: "Did the Messenger of God say it?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then he has spoken the truth." That is, this is a matter above inquiry, and there is no room for employing the intellect in it, because it has a store of truthfulness that places it beyond investigation.

We have already mentioned the essence of the matter regarding these letters. These are the letters in which God mentions the name of the letter, because every letter has a name and a named referent (musammā). For example, the alif's name is "alif," and its referent is a, u, i (the sound it represents). The name is pronounced only by the one who has learned it. The unlettered person does not know the letters ba, ta, tha, but he pronounces them when he speaks.

So: the unlettered person pronounces the referent of the letter and does not know its name. The proof is that when we teach children we say to them, "Spell this word," and they say: "k-t-b." But the unlettered person pronounces it as "kataba" without knowing its letters or their spelling. We have agreed on this point.

Remember that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was unlettered. So what I understand is that (ḥ) is named ḥā, and (m) is named mīm. The proof is that you read at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara (Alif Lam Mim): alif, lam, mim. But at the beginning of al-Sharh you say ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ So why do you read it this way in al-Baqara and that way in al-Sharh?

In al-Baqara you read the name of the letter, while in al-Sharh you read the referent of the letter. Only a learner can distinguish between these. So who taught Muhammad this matter, when the letters are the same letters in the same order?

Another point: the disjoined letters in the Qur'an comprise half of the letters of the alphabet. The alphabet is known to have twenty-eight letters, and the disjoined letters take fourteen of them, distributed in a remarkable way, and scholars remain perplexed in understanding their meanings.

Among the first nine letters, only two are mentioned: alif and ḥā. Among the last nine letters, only seven came, and two did not, in contrast to the first group. As for the ten in the middle, it took the unpointed ones and left the pointed ones: it took sīn and left shīn, took ṣād and left ḍād, took ṭā and left ẓā, took ʿayn and left ghayn. So this is a studied matter, not a random pattern. It is arranged with system and wisdom, like the teeth of a key, so it is a deliberate precision.

Then you see that He, glorified be He, sometimes begins a sura with one letter, like ṣād and qāf; sometimes with two, like ḥā Mīm; sometimes three, like alif lam mim; sometimes four, like alif lam mim ra; and five, like Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf, and Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād. So the matter is a deliberate wisdom, not something without system. It has a purpose: a purpose by which God sets the boundary of the difference between the letters and the rest of speech. How?

They say: the disjoined letters are pronounced as names, and you must pause on them. So you do not say, for example, "alifun lāmun mīmun" joined together. Rather, you say "alif," and stop. "Lām," and stop. "Mīm," and stop. Yet the Qur'an as a whole is built on continuity (waṣl), not on pausing. In Surat al-Raḥmān you say ﴿Both dark green﴾ with the kasra, so that it joins with what follows it: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?﴾

Even the last word of the Qur'an, in Surat al-Nās, you say ﴿of the jinn and of mankind﴾ so that you begin after it and join it to ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾.

But the disjoined letters came built on pausing. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "So..." In the disjoined letters there are purposes and wisdoms that scholars continue to try to reach some of, each according to what God has opened to him of them. As for the letters themselves, they are a treasure that remains and never runs out, from which the Truthful, glorified be He, gives us according to our measure.

They say: the Qur'an came as a stylistic and rhetorical miracle (iʿjāz), and the Arab nation is famous for eloquence and rhetoric. Yet they could not imitate the Qur'an or produce its like, even though God brought it in their language, with their very letters and their expressions, and challenged them with all of this. So they could not produce even one verse like it.

It is as if God were saying to them: "You have the same letters and the same words; why did you not weave from them something like My weaving?" So the aspect of inimitability here is that He, glorified and exalted be He, is the speaker of the Qur'an. He is the one who shaped it and spoke it.

Also, and the meaning that must prevail in all of this: God, the Truthful, has sent down to us creeds and rulings that proceed from the One you believe in and have faith in, and the Qur'an indicates this. These are three: the creeds, which are belief in the Supreme Existence and the Necessary Existent, and that He has absolute attributes of perfection: the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, etc., because these have rational proof established for them.

This wondrous, precisely ordered universe must have a Creator who is powerful, wise, and knowing, etc. So reason supports this creed and establishes it. But these are not all the creeds. There are also matters of transmission (samʿiyyāt), which have no rational proof because they are unseen matters (ghaybiyyāt), as we say, for example: in Paradise there is such-and-such, and its description is such-and-such.

Likewise the punishment of the grave: these are unseen matters. Indeed no rational proof stands for them. Rather, they are protected within what has rational proof. So as long as you have believed in this God, and reason has guided you to Him, take what He has informed you of without debating it. Simply stop at hearing it.

Likewise the rulings, such as prayer, which is the continuous expression of loyalty to God, and zakat, for financial and economic circulation in society, and likewise the pilgrimage to the Sacred House of God. And so on. Rulings too have a rational aspect and a transmitted aspect. Prayer as worship of God and as a sign of loyalty to the One worshipped, glorified be He, is a rational matter. But its manner and the number of its units (rakʿa) are a transmitted matter, which we take as it is and do not debate. Likewise all acts of worship.

Rulings include a rational matter that is understood, and a transmitted matter that is accepted as given. If you say: "How can we stop at matters in religion that are not debated?" We say: Yes, because this stopping at unseen matters is the proof of your faith in God, since rational matters are shared by all people.

We have said: if you have a sum of money that you fear will be stolen, for example, and you placed it under a stone in the garden, and the end of the month came and you wanted, for example, to give your servant his wages from this money. You say to him: "Such-and-such, lift this stone and bring what is beneath it." He says: "I cannot lift it alone, and I will wait for so-and-so to lift it with me." You say to him: "Know that beneath it is the bag with the money from which you will take your wages." Then he goes and lifts the stone alone.

But if you said to another person: "Lift this stone," and he lifted it without asking why, would these two be equal in your obedience?

Likewise with the matter of creeds: there is a difference between one who believes only in rational, sensible matters, and one who believes and accepts even the unseen matter you inform him of.

Likewise the situation regarding creeds, rulings, and the Qur'an: in each there is a rational matter and an unseen matter, and you must refer the unseen matters to the rational ones. The noble Qur'an, and this is our subject, contains speech that is rational and understood by reason, and letters whose meaning is not understood except that God has said them. For this reason we say about them: "And God knows best what He intends by them."

As for His saying: ﴿Ha Mim. A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, I say that this (Ḥā Mīm) is that of which God says ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Since it is a revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, beware of getting involved in it by saying: "What does it mean?" or "It is obscure," etc. Rather, stop at it and take it as God having a meaning in it, and He knows best what He means by it.

Know that after it He says: ﴿A Book whose verses have been detailed﴾. So in the Qur'an there are then both matters: the unseen matter at which one should stop, like (Ḥā Mīm), and these unseen matters are the arena for testing faith; then He also gives you the rational matter that is understood, which He details for you in detail.

The word ﴿revelation﴾ comes from the descent of a thing, and descent occurs from a high place to a place lower than it, or from a higher station to a lower one. This root occurs frequently to indicate the descent of the Qur'an and the method from above, and it occurs in all its derivations: tanzīl, nazala, nunazzil, nazzalnā, anzalnā. ﴿And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended﴾, and He said: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord, with every matter﴾.

Therefore, when you hear the word ﴿revelation﴾, you know that what has come to you is from one higher than you in rank, even if his status is beneath your feet, as He said regarding iron: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might﴾. Iron is known to come from the earth in terms of its origin and formation, yet it is "sent down" from above in terms of its Creator and Giver to you.

So all these derivations of (nazala) indicate the loftiness of the thing sent down. And sent down from whom? ﴿From the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. Therefore you must receive this that is sent down to you with absolute submission and acceptance. For this reason, when they said to our master Abu Bakr: "Your companion claims that he was taken by night to Jerusalem and ascended to heaven," he did not debate this matter rationally. Rather he said to them: "If he said it, then he has spoken the truth."

He made God's word the foundation: if the statement came from him, he is truthful. For this reason, from that day he was given the title al-Siddiq. Although the Night Journey is an earthly sign with a rational aspect, because the distance was known to them, and the manner of travel to Jerusalem was known in time and place, yet he did not debate it. But the Ascension is an unseen matter. So it is as if he made his affirmation of Muhammad in what they know on earth a means to affirming him in what they do not know in heaven.

We also understand from His saying, exalted be He: ﴿A revelation from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ that the obligation which God sent down to you did not come to burden you, but is from a Most Gracious toward you, of vast mercy whose mercy encompasses everything, believer and disbeliever alike.

And (al-Raḥīm) means: one whose mercy is constant, because His mercy, exalted be He, extends and endures even into the Hereafter. So if you see in the revelation an obligation that you think is burdensome, do not understand that it is from one harsh toward you; rather it is from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Gracious toward you, because He guides you to what makes your worldly life and your hereafter happy. The proof is that He, glorified be He, when He obligates us with matters that may be burdensome to the ordinary self, does not benefit from this obligation. Whether you disbelieve or believe, pray or do not pray, He is by His attribute of power existent, whether or not you believe in Him and whether or not you pray.

So your deed has no connection to God in terms of benefit. The benefit is for your own sake, as you say to your son, for example: "If you succeed this year, I will buy you such-and-such."

The word tanzīl (تَنزِيلٌ) [Fuṣṣilat: 2] comes from the descent of a thing (nuzūl), and descent happens from a high place to a place lower than it, or from a higher station to a lower one. This root occurs very often to indicate that the Qur'an and the method (al-manhaj) descend from above, and it comes in all its derivations: tanzīl, nazala, nunazzilu, nazzalnāhu, anzalnā; "and with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended" [al-Isrā': 105], and He said: "The angels and the Spirit descend therein by the permission of their Lord, with every command" [al-Qadr: 4].

Therefore, whenever you hear the word tanzīl [Fuṣṣilat: 2], you know that what has come to you is from one higher than you in rank, even if his station in your eyes is beneath your feet. As He said in al-Ḥadīd: "And We sent down iron, wherein is great might" [al-Ḥadīd: 25]. Iron is known to come from the earth in terms of its origin and formation, yet it is "sent down" from above in terms of its Creator and its Giver to you.

So all these derivations of (nazala) indicate the loftiness of the thing sent down. And sent down from whom? "From the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" [Fuṣṣilat: 2]. Therefore you must receive this thing sent down to you with absolute submission and acceptance...

We also understand from His words, exalted is He, "A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" [Fuṣṣilat: 2], that the obligation which God sent down to you did not come to burden you. Rather, it is from One who is Merciful toward you, of vast mercy, whose mercy "encompasses all things," the believer and the disbeliever alike [al-A'rāf: 156].

And (al-Raḥīm) means: One whose mercy is constant, for the mercy of the Exalted endures and extends even into the Hereafter. So if you see in the revelation an obligation that you think is hard upon you, do not understand that it comes from one who is harsh toward you; rather, it is from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

"Merciful toward you" (raḥmān bika), because He guides you to what makes your worldly life and your Hereafter happy. The proof is that when He, glorified is He, obligates us with matters that may be hard on the ordinary self, He gains nothing from this obligation. Whether you disbelieve or believe, pray or do not pray, He is by His attribute of power existing, even if you do not believe in Him and even if you do not pray.

Thus your deed has no connection to God in terms of benefit; the benefit is for your own sake, just as you say to your son, for example: "If you pass this year, I will buy you such-and-such."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 41, verse 3:

He named it "Kitab" (Book) because kitab means gathering together. The kutaybah (battalion) is a gathering of soldiers, so the kitab gathers words together, and a kitab means: a collection in which things are gathered. In the Qur'an every good of this world and the Hereafter has been gathered. It is a kitab because it is written and recorded; you can read it...

As for the meaning of ﴿fussilat ayatuh﴾ (its verses have been made distinct): they say that the verb "fussilat" is in the passive form, or in the form of what has no named doer. The meaning here is that God made them distinct first, so they became distinct, that is, they became detailed. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) conveyed them to the people, they became detailed explanations of their affairs and their rulings.

Also, the meaning of ﴿fussilat ayatuh﴾: the Qur'an is divided and detailed into surahs, each surah standing on its own, and within the surahs are verses, each verse standing on its own. In the long and the short surahs alike, and likewise in the verses, you find a single word forming a verse and a verse of several lines. Likewise it made the words distinct in terms of their root material; likewise it made the lawful and the unlawful distinct, and obedience and disobedience distinct. Did it not distinguish between promise and threat, between reward and punishment?

The Qur'an has distinguished between all these matters, or every sign of the universe has been detailed in it until the Hour. Therefore they said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave us an eloquent sermon, in which he left nothing out, and there was not a leaf that falls but he told us about it until the Hour arrives. Whoever memorised it memorised it, and whoever forgot it forgot it."

Yes, as God the Exalted said: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38], meaning: the matters that occur in the universe are present for you in this Book...

As for His saying: ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾, that is: in the Arabic tongue and among an Arab nation. But how is that, when it is a universal message for all mankind and for all languages? And why was it not sent down in all languages?... The Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad in his Arab environment, because God the Exalted wanted this religion to appear among an unlettered nation, and through the tongue of an unlettered Messenger, so that no one could say: the Qur'an is a civilizational leap.

The Arabs were a nation without a state to govern them, without a system or a law; they were a group of tribes, each tribe with its own law... Yet this very nation came and united the whole world, with its civilised states, from Persia in the east to Rome in the west.

So from where did this nation obtain that? They had to understand that it was a law of heaven that came from above; otherwise the Arabs would not have been able to carry out this role, had it not been for the message of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Therefore: there is no room to say that Islam is a civilizational leap. Thus, when the Truthful, Glorified God wished to raise His religion, He made Muhammad (ﷺ) proclaim this religion openly in Mecca. Why Mecca in particular? Because Quraysh were there, and it was the seat of leadership in the whole Peninsula, and there were the chieftains whom no one dared confront.

Among these people Muhammad cried out with Islam and proclaimed it openly. Yet these lords did not support the religion; rather, it was supported by the weak and the slaves in Medina. We have said that this matter has a wisdom: that no one should think that tribal partisanship for Muhammad created faith in Muhammad, but rather that faith in Muhammad created tribal partisanship for Muhammad.

So the Qur'an is Arabic because they were the community of the call, who would carry its banner and travel with it throughout the whole world. The Arabs are a people based on wandering; they have no houses, and do not dwell in villas and apartment blocks, but the tent, which he carries with him wherever he goes. His homeland is therefore the whole world, and his house is on the back of his camel. And since they were tribal, each one fanatically loyal to his tribe, wars were numerous among them, to the point that some of them lasted forty years.

These wars trained them in fighting, and planted in them courage and self-sacrifice for the sake of a principle. Therefore, when the Messenger of God wished to prepare an army, he did not have to open a military school; rather, he found a generation of men ready and prepared, who knew all the arts of war. Whenever one of them heard a cry of alarm, he flew to it.

These were the men who would receive the call from the Messenger of God, and they were the ones who would spread it. Therefore the speech must be in their tongue, and the call in their language, so that they could carry it.

For this reason God the Exalted said elsewhere: ﴿We did not send any messenger except with the tongue of his people﴾ [Ibrahim: 4], because they are the ones who would hear from him first.

But how can the religion be universal? They said: when his people hear from him, they believe in him, and then they carry his call to people, not as words, but as a method, a conduct and an example. And it is well known that methods do not differ with languages. Therefore the Muslims conquered the whole world, not by the Qur'an and its verses, but by conduct and by the principles that the Qur'an established.

Thus: the Qur'an was revealed in an Arabic tongue, because the Arabs were the ones prepared for this mission, capable of carrying it, and of travelling with it through the whole world, being a nomadic people who did not settle, a people of fighting; and it is an unlettered nation that cannot be accused of fabricating this religion, or of it being a civilizational leap.

As for His saying: ﴿for a people who know﴾, meaning: who know the methods of the Arabic language, and even excel in it. They were at the highest summit of eloquence and rhetoric, as proof that you will not find a nation on earth that made exhibitions of literature and of the word as the Arabs did at 'Ukaz, al-Mirbad, Dhu al-Majaz and al-Majannah. There they used to display their literary production and evaluate it, and whatever they found admirable of it they honoured by placing it on the curtains of the Ka'bah.

Thus: ﴿for a people who know﴾ Arabic and excel in it to a remarkable degree, such that the miraculous Qur'an was revealed in their tongue. Miraculousness cannot be realised for one who does not excel in the field of miraculousness, for the one who is ignorant of something cannot be challenged in it; rather, miraculousness applies to the skilled person in the thing with which he is challenged, because the ignorant man can say to you: "By God, if I knew that thing, I would have defeated you in it." Hence God challenged the Arabs with the Qur'an.

For this reason, the Truthful, Glorified God does not send down a sign with any of His messengers to prove the truth of his call except of the kind in which the people excelled. Thus the miracle of our master Jesus was in medicine: he would heal the blind and the leper by God's permission; and our master Moses, peace be upon him, had the staff as his miracle, because his people excelled in magic; and the miracle of Muhammad (ﷺ) came in eloquence and clear expression, and he challenged the people with the Qur'an, and by this miraculousness is realised.

Therefore we hear someone say: the Arabs were defeated before the Qur'an. This is not correct, for the Arabs were not defeated but were victorious before the Qur'an. How? Because God the Exalted does not challenge anyone but a strong one; God's challenge to them is evidence that they were a power, possessing the capacity for eloquence and holding the forelock of the language.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 41, verse 4:

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿a bringer of good news and a warner⁠﴾ [Fussilat: 4]. This is the first item of the detailing (tafsil), as we said: He details the truth and falsehood, the lawful and the unlawful, and here (He details) a bringer of good news and a warner. ﴿But most of them turned away, so they do not hear⁠﴾ [Fussilat: 4]. The turning away of the majority indicates that the minority who believed were the weak and oppressed, while most of them were the people of lordship and power, who did not accept the new call that placed them on a level with these weak ones and slaves.

For this reason, when our master Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) assumed the caliphate, a group of these chieftains came to him, and with him were a group of the oppressed who had embraced Islam earlier. He delayed the chieftains and the great ones until he had finished with those who were with him. This grieved them, and they found something in themselves: how could Abu Bakr place slaves and the weak ahead of them? So the Siddiq said: "What is the matter with these people? Each of them is aggrieved that I have placed so-and-so and so-and-so before him. What will they do when Allah places them above them on the Day of Resurrection in Paradise?"

But what is the aspect of the turning away in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But most of them turned away⁠﴾ [Fussilat: 4]? They said: the aspect of the turning away is that they understood what the new religion requires by their saying: "There is no god but Allah."

And that lordship will belong only to this word, and domination will belong only to this word, and that the servants will be equal before it. So how could they say "There is no god but Allah" while they know what it demands? For this reason they did not say it. Had it been merely a word spoken, they would have said it, but they knew its meaning, so they held back.

As for His words: ﴿so they do not hear⁠﴾ [Fussilat: 4], that is, they do not hear a beneficial hearing, or an attentive, accepted hearing. Otherwise, His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But most of them turned away⁠﴾ [Fussilat: 4], indicate that they heard the call of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They heard it with their ears only, and did not benefit from this hearing. For this reason He, Exalted is He, said about them: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until, when they leave your presence, they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he just say?"⁠﴾ [Muhammad: 16].

For this reason people differ in receiving the Qur'an. One listens, is moved, and prostrates before the greatness of the Qur'an, while another listens and says, "What did he say?!", in mockery and disdain. This is because he does not listen with the ear of reflection and contemplation. Why? Because the channels of the heart to the intellect are clouded by what faith requires of them. They have grown accustomed to lordship, so whenever they hear what opposes their lordship and worldly authority, they turn away.

For this reason we have said, regarding the story of the conversion of our master Umar, that when he first heard the Qur'an he was obstinate and raged, because his heart was not prepared for sound reception. When he struck his sister and blood flowed from her, his heart softened and grew gentle, and the haze lifted from him. When he heard the Qur'an, he was affected by it and moved by it, and so he believed.

Meaning of akinna: it means coverings, the plural of kinan, which is a covering. A covering wraps a thing so that light cannot reach it. In another verse He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it﴾ [al-Kahf: 57]. So the coverings are sometimes from God's placing and sometimes from them. Which of the two comes first? Did God place coverings on them first and then heedlessness afflicted them, or was it their turning away from the religion of God that placed the coverings on their hearts?

We have said that when a person becomes accustomed to disbelief and feels at ease with it, God increases him in it and seals his heart, such that faith cannot enter it and disbelief does not leave it.

So: disbelief comes from them first, and after that God seals the heart. Likewise in the matter of the coverings: it came from them first, so God increased them, placed coverings on their hearts, and added sickness to their sickness.

So the meaning of akinna is the coverings that prevent them from understanding and reflecting upon what they hear and what is conveyed to them. ﴿And in our ears is a deafness﴾ — waqr means deafness that prevents hearing. In Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18].

It is well known that muteness arises from deafness, for a deaf person who does not hear, how can he speak? Because language is a social phenomenon and is the daughter of imitation: what the ear hears, the tongue reproduces. If the ear hears nothing, the tongue utters nothing. Language is not innate; language is hearing and imitation, as evidenced by the fact that if you bring an English child, for example, into an Arab environment, he speaks Arabic.

The deaf person has the capacity for speech, as evidenced by his uttering some unintelligible sounds, as we hear from the mute, for example. Even a sound, eloquent normal person cannot speak a word he does not know in his own language; from where would he bring it? From hearing, first.

For this reason we have taken from this matter material proofs of the existence of the Supreme Creator, glorified is He. We say: how do you speak? He says: I speak because in my childhood I heard my father, my mother, and those around me speaking, so I said as they say. So: no language arises except through hearing.

The same holds for the fathers and the grandfathers. Trace this chain back to Adam, peace be upon him, and say: how did Adam speak when there was no one before him to hear from? He must have heard. Heard from whom? He heard from God, the Exalted, when He taught him all the names.

The channels of thoughts that reach the ears, and the channels of thoughts that issue from the tongue: because these are deaf and do not hear, they took nothing, and consequently they produced nothing. Therefore He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings﴾, meaning coverings that prevent them from benefiting, ﴿and in our ears is a deafness﴾, meaning deafness. He did not mention the tongue here. Why? Because they would not speak about the religion, since they had not heard it. His not mentioning speech here shows that they will neither hear nor speak. Reflect on this precision, for it is the speech of a Lord.

As for their saying: ﴿And between us and you is a veil﴾, meaning a thick covering that screens you. When you are with your companion, you talk to him and he talks to you, you hear him and he hears you, you see him and he sees you, you are at ease with him and he is at ease with you, and so on. But if there is a veil between you and him, all of that is prevented.

This veil may be figurative. You say: between so-and-so and so-and-so there is a coolness, meaning a small coolness that soon passes away. But if you say: between so-and-so and so-and-so there is a coolness, and you repeat the adverb of place, this indicates that it is a great coolness, not easy to remove.

Likewise they said: ﴿And between us and you is a veil﴾, meaning a dense, thick covering that conceals everything, from here to here, meaning it fills all the distance between us. They said: when our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), spoke to the people and presented the religion of God, Abu Jahl would take his garment and place it over his face so that he would not see the Messenger of God.

As long as there is a veil between us and you, we will not agree, each of us being on his own path. And as long as each has his own path: ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾. This matter was clarified by the Truthful Lord in Surat al-Kafirun: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshippers of what I worship, nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor are you worshippers of what I worship. For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1-6]. This is the natural result of the veil between them.

Some people, when they read this surah, think it is repetition. This is not repetition; rather, the surah contains the severing of relations, and severing relations has a time that governs it. Do you not see how states sever their relations with one another, and then the atmosphere clears again and relations return better than they were? There is a difference in diplomacy between the past and the present.

But in the matter of disbelief and faith, the situation is different: they are opposites that do not meet, whatever happens in the future. So relations between them will never return. Therefore He, glorified is He, said: ﴿I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 2-3], meaning in the present time, now. ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 4-5], meaning in the future. So do not suppose that relations between us may improve and a bond return between us. No. There is no meeting between us, neither in the present nor in the future.

This is the severing of relations. And as long as there is a veil and a barrier between us, each of us goes his own way (and the bay mare in his horse rides it).

﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾: do what pleases you, and what comes to you from your god and your religion; and we act according to our gods, our religion, and our worship. Act for your God who sent you, and we act for our gods whom we worship; or act for your hereafter and we act for our worldly life. So the matter, from the Messenger, is persistence, and from them, hostility, until the brand is straightened, and God refuses except to complete His light.

Thus we see the gradualness of Islam and its slow spread. He commanded its followers to emigrate to Abyssinia and to Medina. He led them gradually until their strength grew. It began weak, with the weak, then grew strong until the strong entered. It was confined to Mecca, then its circle widened, and it increased every day, so that the land of Islam grew and the land of disbelief diminished.

Therefore, when Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-As saw the spread of Islam in this manner, Khalid said to Amr: "By God, the brand has indeed been straightened," meaning the affair of this religion has become firm, so come, let us embrace Islam. And the leaders of disbelief began returning to the right path and entering the religion of God...

(Say) — that is, in replying to them: "I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed that your God is one God."

Meaning: why do you stand against me and my call with such obstinacy? Why do you place veils between me and you, when I am one of you, an Arab like you, whose truthfulness and history you have known before this, living among you?

And by Allah's mercy toward you, He sent me to you as a human being of your own kind, and did not send an angel to you: "And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have covered them with that which they cover" [al-An'am: 9]. You know his past in truthfulness, trustworthiness and chastity. Then, even if an angel came to you, would you follow him in his angelhood? Indeed, a model cannot be an angel for humans.

Consider the good manners and humility of the Messenger of Allah in his saying: "I am only a human being like you." That is: there is no arrogance and no haughtiness; rather, Allah has favoured me over you by revealing to me... and the content of this revelation is that "your God is one God." And since it is revealed to me, I am only a conveyer, and I bear no blame that you may hold me accountable for. I am a human being like you and from among yourselves; I am distinguished from you only by what Allah has distinguished me with, namely revelation.

Therefore we find that the Exalted often corrects His Messenger, adjusts his ruling for him and admonishes him, and the Messenger himself is the one who informs us of this, which is evidence that he was faithful in conveying from his Lord. Hence He, the Exalted, says: "And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have severed from him the aorta" [al-Haqqah: 44–46].

And He said "your God" (ilahukum) and did not say "your Lord" (rabbukum), because they affirm the existence of God the Creator, the Provider; the problem for them lies in the God who is worshipped. The worshipped God has commands and requirements; divinity entails obedience in what is commanded and in what is forbidden. They acknowledge Lordship but associate others in Divinity. So He willed to make clear to them: "your God is one God" — not multiple. In one place He says "one God," and in Surat al-Ikhlas He says: "Say: He is Allah, the One (Ahad)" [al-Ikhlas: 1]. "One" means that He has no second; "Ahad" means that He is one in His essence, not composed of parts, so it negates divisibility.

The disbelievers adopted many gods to satisfy the religious sentiment within themselves, and so that they would have a worshipped god without a method and without obligations. Therefore we have said: among the moderation of our religion is that it believes in one God, whereas some believe in many gods, and some deny God altogether; then the Islamic religion came and explained that God is one.

Since He is one God: "So take the straight path to Him and seek His forgiveness" — "istaqim" means: proceed along the line of uprightness, not inclining here or there. It is said: a man from Tayy, named Ibn Bandar, saw a young man whose house was here, but he did not go to it by the usual straight road; rather he circled through the village lanes to reach his house. So he (Ibn Bandar) understood from that that the young man, by his circling through the lanes, intended something suspicious, and he said to him: "O such-and-such, go straight to your house," meaning: go to it by the straight road. Then the young man realised that the man had understood his improper intention, and he desisted.

Likewise His saying: "So take the straight path to Him" means: aim for Him by the way of uprightness. He called His way "the straight path," and science has established that the straight path is the shortest distance between two points. Moreover, a straight path may be narrow, compelling you to keep to it, or it may be wide, allowing you to lean right and left; if it is wide, keep straight in it too, so that you shorten the distance of arrival for yourself, for when you lean you increase the distance. Therefore He said: "the even way" [al-Baqarah: 108], meaning in its middle without inclination, such that what is on your right is like what is on your left. So once He said: "Guide us to the straight path" [al-Fatihah: 6], and once He said: "the even way" [al-Baqarah: 108].

So His saying "take the straight path to Him" means: at the beginning. If heedlessness of the method overtakes you and you commit something, then "seek His forgiveness" — that is, ask Him for forgiveness.

"And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat" — because seeking forgiveness is a request for the erasure of what preceded. The legal principle says: warding off harm takes precedence over securing benefit. We have given an example of this: one man wants to throw you an apple, and another wants to throw a stone at you; which is preferable? The preferable is to repel the stone. So He said "and seek His forgiveness," so that the erasure of sins may be completed for you, and so that you may establish with God a new relationship founded on obedience and uprightness.

The word "woe" (wayl) means destruction. "To the polytheists, who do not give zakat": was zakat obligatory upon a polytheist? Zakat had not yet been made obligatory even upon the believers at that time. It is said: what is meant by zakat here is the purification of wealth in its growth, and the polytheists were in fact doing this, but they did it out of generosity and the pursuit of a good reputation, and God was not in their minds...

And His saying, glorified is He: "and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers" means: they disbelieved at the outset when they associated partners with the One God, and they disbelieved at the end in the Hereafter; they disbelieved at the source and at the outcome.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 41, verse 7:

(Say) that is, in replying to them: ﴿Say: I am only a man like you; it is revealed to me...﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. That is: why do you stand against me and my call with this obstinate stance? Why do you place veils between me and you, when I am one of you, an Arab like you, whom you know for my truthfulness and my history before this, living among you?

Among God's mercy to you is that He sent me to you as a human being of your own kind, and did not send you an angel: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have covered for them what they cover [themselves in confusion]﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. You also know his precedents in truthfulness, trustworthiness and chastity. Then, if an angel had come to you, would you have followed him in his angelic nature? Indeed, exemplary conduct cannot come from an angel to humans.

Consider the courtesy and humility of the Messenger of God in his saying: ﴿I am only a man like you...﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. That is: there is no pride or haughtiness; rather, God has favoured me over you by ﴿it is revealed to me...﴾ [Fussilat: 6], and the content of this revelation is ﴿that your God is one God...﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. And since it is revealed to me, I am a conveyor with no fault for which you may hold me to account. I am a human being like you, from among yourselves; I am distinguished above you only by what God has distinguished me with, namely revelation.

Therefore we find that the Truth, glorified is He, often corrects His Messenger, adjusts his judgement for him and rebukes him, and the Messenger himself is the one who tells us of this, which is evidence that he is trustworthy in conveying from his Lord. So He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44-46].

He said ﴿your God [ilahakum]﴾ [Fussilat: 6] and did not say "your Lord [rabbakum]" because they believe in the existence of God the Creator, the Provider; the problem for them lies in the worshipped deity (ilah). The worshipped deity has commands and requirements; deity entails obedience in what is commanded and in what is forbidden. They affirm lordship (rububiyyah) but associate others in deity (uluhiyyah). So He wished to make clear to them: ﴿that your God is one God...﴾ [Fussilat: 6], not plural. Once He says ﴿one God...﴾ [Fussilat: 6], and in the surah of Sincerity He says ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]: "one" means He has no second, and "One" (ahad) means He is one in His essence, not composed of parts; so these words negate division.

The disbelievers have taken many gods to satisfy what is in themselves of the impulse of religiosity, and so that they may have a worshipped deity without a method and without obligations. Therefore we have said that among the moderation of our religion is that it believes in one God, whereas some believe in many gods, and some deny God altogether; then the Islamic religion came and explained that God is one.

And since He is one God: ﴿so go straight towards Him and seek His forgiveness...﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. "Istaqim" means: proceed along the line of straightness, not inclining here or there. It is said: a man from Tayy, named Ibn Bandar, saw a young man whose house was here, but he did not go to it by the usual straight road; rather he went round the village lanes to reach his house.

So he understood from that that the young man, by his wandering through the lanes, intended something suspicious, so he said to him: "O you, go straight to your house", that is: go to it by the straight road. Then the young man realised that the man had seen through him (fasahsahu) and understood his dishonourable intent, and he desisted.

Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so go straight towards Him...﴾ [Fussilat: 6], that is: make for Him by the way of uprightness. He called His path "the straight path", and science has established that the straight path is the shortest distance between two points. Moreover, the straight path may be narrow, forcing you to keep to it, or it may be wide, permitting leaning to the right and left (an autostrade).

If it is wide, then keep straight in it too, so that you shorten the distance of arrival for yourself, for when you lean you increase the distance. Therefore He said: ﴿the even way [sawa' al-sabil]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108], that is: in its middle, without inclination, such that what is on your right is like what is on your left. So once He said ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6] and once He said ﴿the even way﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108].

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so go straight towards Him...﴾ [Fussilat: 6], that is: at the outset. If heedlessness of the method befalls you and you commit something, ﴿and seek His forgiveness...﴾ [Fussilat: 6], that is: ask Him for forgiveness.

﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give the zakah...﴾ [Fussilat: 6-7], because seeking forgiveness is a request for the erasure of what has preceded, and the legal principle says: averting harm takes precedence over securing benefit. We illustrate this with someone who wants to throw you an apple, and someone who wants to throw a stone at you: which is preferable? The preferable thing is to repel the stone. So He said ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾ [Fussilat: 6] so that the erasure of sins may be completed for you, and so that you may establish with God a new relationship founded on obedience and straightness.

The word ﴿woe [wayl]﴾ [Fussilat: 6] means ruin, ﴿to the polytheists, who do not give the zakah...﴾ [Fussilat: 6-7]. Was zakah prescribed for a polytheist? Zakah had not yet been prescribed even for the believers at this time. They said: the intended meaning of zakah here is the purification of wealth at the stage of its growth, and the polytheists were indeed doing this, but they did it out of generosity and the desire for a good reputation, and God was not in their minds.

Hence it is related that al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi had a cooking pot in which he fed such-and-such, to the extent that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said... and similarly Hatim al-Ta'i and other generous Arabs; but He said: ﴿who do not give the zakah﴾ [Fussilat: 7], because a person usually loves his wealth, and the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, those are the successful﴾ [al-Hashr: 9], because a human has many demands in life.

Buying and selling was a barter of goods: you give me a commodity, and I give you in exchange another commodity, at a time when money did not yet exist: you give me wheat, and I give you dates, for example; each of these things is both a price and a commodity. The wheat with you is a commodity, and the dates with me are a price. So each one of us is both a seller and a buyer.

Therefore He, exalted is He, said in the story of Prophet Joseph: ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his residence honourable..."﴾ [Yusuf: 21]; so He said "bought him" (ishtarahu), meaning he took him, and of the others He said: ﴿and they sold him for a meagre price, a few counted dirhams...﴾ [Yusuf: 20], meaning they sold him. So this is an exchange; each of them was a seller and a buyer at the same time.

﴿Those who do not give the zakah and who, of the Hereafter, are disbelievers﴾ [Fussilat: 7]. Or is this a general word? By their polytheism they did not take on God's ruling regarding zakah, so there was no good left in them for their surroundings or their fellow citizens, because God, exalted is He, wants faith to spread mutual support among mankind: the strong helping the weak, the healthy helping the sick, the rich helping the poor, the learned helping the ignorant.

But the most important aspect of life is the aspect of sustaining life with sustenance, and sustenance requires wealth. Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, when He speaks on this matter, speaks of "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum), who are people whose hearts we want to soften towards the religion of God, and to draw them to it so that they may examine and choose well, not that we buy them for the religion as some claim.

Among the ways to this end is that we treat them well; therefore God made them one of the channels of zakah, and gave them from God's wealth so that their hearts were softened.

And when you do good to a person, what have you done to him? First, you have shaken off his hatred; and as long as you have shaken off his hatred, he does not look at you while hating you or harbouring spite against you, and at the least he listens to you. This is what happened with those whose hearts were to be reconciled.

Therefore when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed away, a group of Arabs apostatised from the religion of God. Why? The first thing they apostatised over was the obligation of zakah, and because of it were the wars of apostasy (ridda). Thus we heard that Sajah, a claimant to prophethood, and Musaylimah, when they first made their claims, said: "We shall remove zakah from you," so that by this they might gain acceptance for their alleged prophethood, desiring by it to lighten the obligations that burden the self.

Some of them said: "We shall remove half the prayer from you." Every lightening of God's law is null and harmful, because it descends from the method of God to the method of lightening, whereas God, glorified is He, when He wants lightening and ease, brings the ease from Himself, and the method of God cannot be corrected.

In God's law there are many rulings showing such lightening, such as the fasting of the sick and the traveller, and the prayer of the sick and the traveller, and much else in the law. So God, the Lawgiver, is the one who determines the lightening for you, not you, and He, glorified is He, knows best the extent of hardship that requires the easing of the ruling.

Therefore we hear someone say: "We want to renew Islam." We say: Glory be to God! O people, fear God. How can we renew Islam? How can we correct God's rulings? And we say: "O Shaykh, renew what you wish; no Muslim will wear your new garment," the reason being that the garment of piety from the Creator does not wear out until a creature renews it. Let yourselves rest.

But why did God make some people rich and others poor and needy? Why did He not make them all in ease, so that there would be no need for zakah? They said: because God wants to spread among His creation mercy and affection; when the poor man finds the rich man does not look down on him because of his wealth, but comes to him and knocks on his door, and gives him his right in God's wealth, then he loves him and wishes him good and more, does not harbour envy towards him, and does not wish the blessing to be removed from his hands.

So: when you give, you draw out anger and envy from souls, and so you make your wealth subject to increase. God, exalted is He, is able to make all people rich, but the wisdom lies in that the rich and the poor exist, and that this matter circulates, for the wealth of the rich may not last, nor the poverty of the poor, as conditions turn, so that each becomes bound to the other by a bond of love and affection, and the bond here is not a bond of favour but a bond of need.

If we all graduated from the university, who would sweep the street, who would drive the car, who would make for us this and that? You say: we may agree that each of us does some work on a specified day.

We say: yes, but the work then becomes a favour, and a favour binds no one; need is what binds. God wants people's interests to be bound by need. Therefore you find a man doing a hard task, perhaps harmful, which you may not bear, and you may regard this work as base; what moved him to it? Need moved him, and the necessities of life, earning a livelihood, and responsibility for family and children compelled him to it; otherwise he would not have humiliated himself thus.

And by God, we have seen in one household a man working as a "sarmati" (a seller of dried goods?) and his brother selling perfumes; consider what each of them smells of.

Our master, Shaykh Musa, may God be pleased with him, often used to supplicate and say: "O God, impoverish the craftsmen and enrich the scholars." We used to be angry at this supplication and say to him: "What are you saying, our master? How so?" He would say: "By God, if the scholars became poor they would slip in their fatwas, and if the craftsmen became rich we would gain nothing from them."

Indeed we have seen that the worker, if he has ten pounds in his pocket, sits idle until he spends them. So: need is necessary for the affairs of creation to be settled.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, made the circulation of wealth in society the most important issue in Islam, and therefore made it one of the pillars of Islam. God did not exempt anyone from extending the hand of economic circulation to others: if he has means, let him give; and if he has no means of wealth, let him find words of counsel to offer to whoever has means.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿No blame lies on the weak, nor on the sick, nor on those who do not find what to spend, if they are sincere to God and His Messenger. There is no way against the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

If he has neither wealth nor the words that soften hearts, then at least let him do this in his own person: ﴿nor on those who came to you that you might mount them; you said, "I find no mount for you," they turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears in grief that they could not find what to spend﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92], that is, in jihad.

This is the third stage: if he has means, let him give; if he has none, let him give the words that soften the hearts of those who have means; and finally, if he finds neither, he grieves within himself that he has nothing; his self yearns to give but he cannot, and his longing in this matter reaches the point that he weeps in pain and sorrow for his yearning for giving.

All of this concerns the circulation of wealth and the economy in Islamic society, for it is the sinew of life, by which life is sustained and by which sustenance comes.

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and of the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾ [Fussilat: 7], it means: they disbelieved at the beginning when they associated partners with the One God, and they disbelieved at the end in the Hereafter; they disbelieved at the source and at the outlet.

Mention of the opposite is one of the characteristics of the Qur'anic style. After mentioning the disbelievers, He mentioned after them those who believed and did righteous deeds, and He did not leave the matter in this vague state; rather, He set the two images before you so that you may compare and judge, as in: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, * And indeed, the wicked will be in the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Infitar: 13-14].

And He said: ﴿So let them laugh a little and let them weep much...﴾ [al-Tawbah: 82].

This is so that the comparison may be complete in its time.

The meaning of ﴿mamnun﴾ [Fussilat: 8] is: uninterrupted (ghayr munqati'). Or "mamnun" means: He does not bestow it upon them as a favour (la yamunnu bihi 'alayhim), as in: ﴿And indeed, for you there is a reward never cut off﴾ [al-Qalam: 3]. In this there is another point: the one who does a righteous deed, and then his affairs prevent him from doing it, Allah says to him: "The incapacity in you is from Me; therefore I will give you the reward of what you used to do previously, and its reward will continue for you until the Day of Resurrection." This is the meaning of ﴿ghayr mamnun﴾ [Fussilat: 8].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 41, verse 9:

The context here shifts to considering the signs of the universe, because they are the means to faith in the One who brought it into being, glory be to Him. The universe is a wondrous, marvelous creation, perfect in its order and in its design. This order is stable: it does not deviate, and nothing arises in it that would take it out of this perfection. So if you wish to soften people's hearts, remind them of the natural cosmic signs in which man has no part.

For this reason you find frequently in the Qur'an: ﴿And of His signs...﴾ [al-Shura: 32].

Here He speaks to us of the first creation and the beginning of the emergence of this earth: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days...﴾ The hamza here conveys the interrogative of denial, which rejects their disbelief in the Creator, glory be to Him, as if He were saying to them: this act of yours is known to Us and is not permissible. He wants to draw their attention to the alternative.

Then they did not content themselves with disbelief in the Creator, but ﴿and you set up rivals to Him﴾, meaning: partners, even though they know that He alone is the Creator: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87]. ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah." Say: "All praise is for Allah." But most of them do not know﴾ [Luqman: 25].

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 41 (Fussilat), verses 10–11:

The Truth, glory be to Him, spoke of the creation of the earth and informed us that He created it in two days. Does this mean that the creation of the earth took two days by our days? No. Beware of thinking that the creation of the earth took two days, or that it was a process requiring time.

The matter is like when you say, for example: "I want to make yogurt at home, so I say to you: bring the milk and add the known culture for making yogurt, then leave it at a certain temperature for a certain period, and after that the milk becomes yogurt after several hours, for example." Does this mean that making the yogurt took you several hours? No, rather it was minutes in which you prepared the ingredient and left it to react until it became yogurt.

For example, when you go to the tailor to have him sew you a garment, he tells you: "Come and take it after a week." Did the garment remain in his hand for a week? Likewise is this matter of creation.

And after God created the earth, He placed in it the rawasi (ar-rawasi), which are the firmly fixed, stable mountains by which the earth is steadied, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And the mountains as pegs﴾ [An-Naba': 7]. Had the earth been stable by its own nature, it would not have needed the mountains. Thus the rawasi indicate that the earth rotates; this is evidence for the rotation of the earth.

﴿And He blessed in it...﴾ [Fussilat: 10]. We have said: blessing (barakah) is that a thing gives forth good beyond its apparent size and beyond what is expected of it, as when you find food that you thought would suffice for five sufficing for ten, and you say: "There is blessing in it."

And regarding His saying ﴿And He blessed in it...﴾ [Fussilat: 10], in what? In the earth, since it was mentioned first? Or in the mountains, which are mentioned last? They said: ﴿And He blessed in it...﴾ [Fussilat: 10] means: in the rawasi. ﴿And He determined in it its sustenance...﴾ [Fussilat: 10] means: in the mountains also.

Reality has confirmed this, and science has established that the mountains are the source of goodness for the rest of the earth, and from them come the elements of fertility and the nourishment without which the life of living beings cannot persist. It is well known that the elements in the soil are depleted and need replenishment and renewal from time to time.

This is indeed what happens: when rain falls on the mountains, it crumbles their surface, and the torrent carries this debris and moves it to distribute it over the flat cultivated land, as in the Nile silt of old, before the building of the High Dam. From where did this silt come? From the sources of the Nile in the high mountains.

We used to see the water of the Nile like tahini, and it would remain so until its outflow into the Mediterranean Sea. From this silt the Delta arose; the sea used to extend as far as Damietta, and now look at what lies between Damietta and Ras al-Bar, for example.

Likewise is the situation in the valleys around the mountains, where the agents of erosion affect the outer crust of the mountains, and the torrent sweeps it into the valleys, so the soil is renewed and its fertility increases. Thus the mountains are truly storehouses of the people's sustenance, and for this reason He said of them ﴿And He blessed in it...﴾ [Fussilat: 10].

Consider also the wisdom and the lofty cosmic engineering: the mountain's base is below and its peak is above, contrary to the valley between two mountains, where the apex of the triangle points downward and its base upward. Every year the rain comes to take from the mountain's peak and give to the base of the valley, as if it were a renewal and widening of the valley suited to the growth of the human population.

God, exalted is He, gives of His bounty in proportion to the increase that now frightens us; that is, be reassured, for provision is guaranteed with God. Therefore He said after it ﴿And He determined in it its sustenance...﴾ [Fussilat: 10].

These stages: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed in it, and determined in it its sustenance...﴾ [Fussilat: 10] came within ﴿four days...﴾ [Fussilat: 10]. These four days are ﴿equal...﴾ [Fussilat: 10], i.e., equal days, ﴿for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat: 10], i.e., those seeking provision.

Or ﴿in four days...﴾ [Fussilat: 10] means: in the completion of four days, ﴿equal...﴾ [Fussilat: 10], i.e., they were balanced and completed.
