The Truth, glory be to Him, praises the station of calling to Allah and makes it the best of what a person can say: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾. So the most noble of deeds for one whose heart is filled with faith is that he should transmit this faith to others, and convey to them the image of faith. The believer does good for himself and for people, because the good of people returns to him as well, just as their evil must inevitably reach him and befall him as its share.

So: it is in your interest, O believer, that people believe, and it is in your interest, O one who is upright on the path, that people become upright. For this reason Allah has entrusted the trust of calling to Him to every believer, because He, glory be to Him, wants faith to be passed from those who have tasted it to those who have not tasted it, so that the expanse of faith widens and goodness becomes general for all.

The first elements of calling to Allah are that we call to belief first and to faith in Allah: that we say, "Our Lord is Allah," affirming it and declaring it sincerely without hesitation. Then we draw their attention to the signs of Allah in the universe, to the cosmic signs if they do not reflect upon them, and to the signs of the miracles accompanying the messengers if they do not know them. Then (we direct them) to the signs of the Wise Reminder, which carry the method of Allah: "do" and "do not."

Consider His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And who is better in speech﴾. The Truth, glory be to Him, wished to make clear to us the station of calling to Allah and the virtue of the caller, but He did not do so in a declarative style that establishes this station; rather He came with this question, ﴿And who is better in speech﴾, a question whose purpose is negation. That is: no one is better than this one who calls to Allah, and there is no speech better than his speech.

He, glory be to Him, said it in the form of a question because He knows that there is no answer to it except that we say: no one is better in speech than one who calls to Allah. Thus He made us declare this truth and affirm it, and affirmation, as they say, is "the master of proofs."

The first caller to Allah is our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and every caller after him draws from his spring and walks in his footsteps. Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was the last of the prophets, he left to his community this mission, the mission of calling to Allah with wisdom and good admonition. So the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) legacy has not ended but extends through his community after him, and every caller after him takes a station from his station (ﷺ).

Among Allah's mercy upon this community is that He made for it a restraint from within itself: He placed in it a group that remains upon the truth, straightening the crooked, commanding good and forbidding evil, and this group will continue until the Day of Resurrection. For this reason there came in the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "A group of my community will continue to be victorious upon the truth; those who oppose them will not harm them until the command of Allah comes while they are still so."

For this reason He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

This is a distinction that Allah has singled out for the community of Muhammad, because he is the Seal of the Messengers; therefore evil will not engulf this community, and corruption will not overspread it, for it has a safeguard from within itself. Previous nations, corruption would take root among them until it encompassed them, so there would be no one enjoining good or forbidding evil, and then it was necessary to send a new messenger to bring people back to the straight path.

As for the community of Muhammad, no new messenger will come among them; therefore Allah placed in them this safeguard, made them a successor to the Messenger of Allah in calling to Allah, and made them trustees of this call. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) says: "Goodness is in me and in my community until the Day of Resurrection."

Allah the Exalted has also made clear that the Messenger will bear witness that he conveyed this call to his community, and this community will bear witness that it conveyed the call of its Messenger to all nations. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle community, that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

So our witness over the nations is evidence that goodness remains within us and will never end.

Our Messenger (ﷺ) also urged us to bear this trust and encouraged us to it when he said (ﷺ): "May Allah make radiant the face of a man who hears my saying, memorizes it, and conveys it to one who has not heard it, for many a bearer of knowledge conveys it to one more understanding than the hearer."

Calling to Allah is a wide field: it happens through speech, through action, and through good example. It happens through explaining the beliefs, acts of worship and rulings to people in an engaging, pleasant and attractive manner, one that does not repel people and does not lead them to despair or hopelessness of Allah's mercy.

Calling to Allah is an art. Read His saying, addressing His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159].

Where are our callers in relation to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl: 125].

We must know that calling to Allah is not the task of specialized religious scholars alone, but the task of every Muslim in every age and every place. Each person, in his field of work, can be a caller: indeed, a caller through his conduct, his commitment, his dedication and his sincerity.

The scholars of the community have agreed that Islam did not spread by the edge of the sword, nor by force as much as it spread through the good conduct of Muslims and their tolerance and love for others, and for us in them there is an example.

Calling to Allah is the task of every Muslim who has tasted the sweetness of faith and the pleasure of obligations, and who loves for people the good that he loves for himself, and so conveys it to them. When the Truth, glory be to Him, charges us with goodness, He does not leave anyone out or deprive anyone of having a share in this goodness... There is an issue connected with calling to Allah: that one of us may be disobedient to his Lord in some respect, so does this disobedience prevent him from being a caller to Allah? They said: disobedience should not prevent you from calling, for perhaps the one you call will do what you have not done, and perhaps this is a process of compensating for the deficiency in you.

It is related that a man was circumambulating the House, and he heard another saying: "O Allah, You know that I disobey You, but I love those who obey You, so make my love for those who obey You an intercessor for my disobedience."

They said: even one who is lax in prayer is not prevented by that from calling others to prayer, because it is goodness that he spreads among people, and its reward will not be withheld from him. Whoever spreads some goodness has a reward with Allah; thus no creature is free of Allah's vast grace reaching him, and no creature is without some quality of goodness, for himself or for others, and this spreading of goodness in itself is a call to Allah.

As for His saying, ﴿and does righteousness﴾, it means: he calls to Allah by speech and then by action. The Qur'an constantly joins speech and action, and we know that the example of action has a greater effect on souls than the example of speech. It is not proper for you to call people to something while you yourself turn away from it. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44]... And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims."﴾ This is a declaration that the Muslim makes and takes pride in, a sash upon his chest: I am a Muslim, and my Islam is the starting point through which my movement in life takes place. This in itself is a call to Allah, a spreading of the religion of Allah, and an elevation of the word of Allah, when you are not occupied with yourself but occupied with your religion.

If you accomplish a work that you attribute to the religion of Allah, saying: "Because Allah commanded me," you raise the religion of Allah in people's eyes and do not concern yourself with your own acting self; and when you raise the religion of Allah, be certain that He raises you along with it.

So: among the qualities of the believer is that he attributes his good and his righteousness to his religion and his Islam.

For this reason we pause often at the saying of Qarun when Allah gave him wealth, status and power, and he said: ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I possess﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. Allah replied to him: since you were given it on knowledge you have, then preserve it with your knowledge; and the outcome was ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾ [al-Qasas: 81]. So when you reach an innovation, an invention, or a reform in the universe, make it from the starting point of religion and method, attribute it to your religion...

We have said: work is either for Allah or for people. Work for Allah has as its condition sincerity, and its reward is with Allah in the Hereafter; as for work for people, it gives you a station among them, prestige and eminence. That is your reward, and you have taken it in this world, so you have no share in the reward of the Hereafter; a person seeks his reward from the one for whom he worked.

For this reason, we are not asked about scholars who served humanity through their inventions, achievements and innovations: do they have a share in the Hereafter? We say: no, they have no share, because they acted for people and for humanity and for the advancement of society, and they took their wages in renown, reputation, fame and the perpetuation of their memory, and so on.

As for Allah, He was never in their minds when they did these things. Read His saying regarding such people: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23].

And in another place He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved, their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert, which the thirsty one thinks is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing; but he finds Allah with him, and He pays him in full his account. And Allah is swift in account﴾ [al-Nur: 39].

Thus are the deeds of the disbelievers in the Hereafter like a mirage: you think it is something, but when you go to it you do not find it. Would that their matter ended at this point, but they are confronted with the reality that they denied in the world:

﴿and he finds Allah with him﴾ [al-Nur: 39]. Yes, Allah, whom he denied or disbelieved in, stops him and calls him to account: "You did it so that it would be said, and it was said, so there is no reward for you with Me," and there remains for you the requital of your disbelief and obstinacy.

So: we say, when you declare that you work and innovate from the starting point of your Islam, when you say, "I worked because I am a Muslim," you exalt the standing of Islam and draw the attention of non-Muslims to the beauty of this religion, and in that you are a caller to Allah, upon the path of your Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). If some hardships confront you, then be patient, for your Messenger was harmed in the cause of his call and he was patient.

Whoever bears the trust of calling and declares it, "I am a Muslim, and my Islam is the governing principle of all my movements in life," and suffers some harm, knows that he has taken a portion of the inheritance of prophethood, for no prophet has been harmed without having enemies. Those who bear this responsibility must have enemies, and be insulted, and have accusations heaped upon them; this is a natural matter in the course of calling to Allah.

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils among mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorated speech as deception﴾ [al-An'am: 112].

This means that the caller who is spared this harm has a diminished share of the inheritance of prophethood, and a diminished share of the legacy of the Prophet (ﷺ). So: be patient. And is the follower of Muhammad better than Muhammad, that he should be spared harm?

If you have no enemies on the path of calling, know that you are not on the path that the bearer of the call has laid out for you, and you should examine yourself.

The discussion here concerns calling to Allah in truth, detachment and sincerity, and about the word spoken for the sake of Allah, not for the sake of rank, authority or a position of the fleeting goods of this world. Calling to Allah is never a bridge (to worldly ends).

For this reason we say: what protects the callers to Allah now? Here we are, saying it at the top of our voices and writing in every medium, and Allah is the Protector; praise be to Allah, we have not been seized, nor imprisoned, nor has anyone confronted us. Many religious scholars declare the word of truth, stripped of desire and interest, and when the ruler gives them his ear, they tell him things that make him tremble; yet we hear of the persecution of religious men.

We say: if a religious man is persecuted, then he must have used forbidden means in calling to Allah, like those who incline to solving problems by killing and bloodshed. Are you in dispute, for example, with one of the ministers, so you strike him with fire? Is this the solution? And what is the fault of the guards whose blood is wasted and whose children are made orphans?

You are a person of words: say what you wish, and reform by good speech; make them hear what they dislike. We have already said to them what no one else could say to them, for the courage of faith in calling to Allah is not a word of truth said against a ruler, but a word of truth said in the presence of an unjust ruler, yes, in his very presence.

This is a practical application of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The greatest jihad is a word of truth before an unjust ruler."

We do not trade in the word; rather we confront with it every ruler who is oppressive. We say to him: we do not hate you, nor do we covet what is in your hand of rule; rather we love you and want to help you in your task. We only want you to rule us by Islam; I want to be ruled by Islam, not that I be ruled by Islam [sic].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 41, verse 34:

After Allah, glorified is He, has told us about the task of calling to Allah, and that it is the inheritance of the prophets and the legacy the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left us after him, He teaches us here an art of da'wah (calling to Islam) and a lesson from its lessons, namely repelling evil with good: ﴿And good and evil are not equal...﴾ [Fussilat: 34].

Yes, no one equates good and evil, and reason affirms this. Come to the thief who steals people's wealth and takes the fruit of their sweat, and say to him: Would you like people to steal from you? He says: No. We say: Then do not wish for them what you do not wish for yourself. He says to you: You restrict my freedom, and I am free.

We say to him: Do not forget that Allah restricted your freedom to steal from others, though you are one individual, and He restricted the movement of the whole world so that it does not steal from you. So who benefits? Likewise, in matters of the Shari'ah, where Allah has forbidden you to transgress against others, He has forbidden them all to transgress against you. He says to you: Do not look at what Allah has forbidden you with desire, and He commands all people not to look at your forbidden things.

The Prophet (ﷺ) gives us a model of the wisdom of da'wah, when the young man said: "By Allah, I have never intended to look at anything without remembering my mother, my sister, my wife and my daughter."

So: the religion, in calling to it, needs gentleness, wisdom and good admonition, so that what you say is accepted from you, because the one you advise regarding a matter of religion, who is not of your religion, or who is of your religion but has grown accustomed to disobedience and finds obedience burdensome, you should remove him from what he is accustomed to by a method that he does not dislike, so that you do not combine hardship upon him when you strip him of what he loves. Harshness of method and coarseness, it is enough that you remove him from what he loves with what he does not dislike, and by this you prevent him from the fierceness of argument, the fury of stubbornness and arrogance.

Likewise in dealing with people: you must confront evil with good: ﴿Repel with that which is better...﴾ [Fussilat: 34], meaning: respond with gentleness and kindness, ﴿and thereupon the one between you and him enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. Destructive enmity is that which exists between two enemies, each of whom is the enemy of the other; in this case hostility spreads and becomes entrenched, and we do not reach a solution in it. So when is the sharpness of enmity broken?

Its sharpness is broken when it comes from one side only: one side is an enemy, and the other side is forbearing, who does not return evil with evil but pardons and forgives. In this case the enemy's soul calms, and he finds no room for his enmity. This is the first step of reform: that you take your enemy by your side. Therefore they say: Do not requite one who disobeys Allah regarding you with more than that you obey Allah regarding him.

In this way the enemy turns into ﴿a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34], meaning: a close, loving, sincere friend. How? Do not ask how; it is by the power of Allah, the Creator of these souls and these hearts and their Turner.

A man came complaining of the harshness of one of his relatives, so we said to him: O shaykh, be patient with him, meet him with what is better, and show him affection, perhaps Allah will set right what is between you two. Afterward he came and said: I repelled with what is better, but he only increased in harshness and became worse than he was. I said to him: Then examine yourself, for the word of Allah is an established matter, and look for the cause within yourself. Perhaps you thought you had repelled with what is better, while in reality you had not repelled with what is better, or you wanted to test Allah, and Allah, exalted is He, is not to be tested; testing Allah is doubt. If you were sincere with Allah, Allah would be sincere with you.

How beautiful is the poet's saying on this meaning:

O you whom the deeds of the one and the other distress, repel, may I be ransomed for you, with that which is better, until you see that the one...

This is the same quality and the same rank: repelling evil with what is better. Only those who are patient under harm attain it, and none reaches it except one of great fortune. That is, a generous share of bounty. Why? Because he restrained his soul and held it back from repaying in kind. When he suppressed his soul for the sake of God, God made its outcome good and gave him abundant reward.

Here in the Qur'anic expression we notice the repetition of the phrase "wa ma yulaqqaha" (and it is not bestowed). God, glory be to Him, did not say: "And it is not bestowed except upon those who are patient and [the one of] great fortune." They said: the phrase is repeated because the receiving is different. This is a receiving through patience, and that is a receiving through reward... "Wa ma yulaqqaha illa alladhina sabaru" (And it is not bestowed except upon those who are patient): patient under injury, patient in controlling the self, and patient in overcoming Satan, who whispers to them to seek revenge and makes repaying in kind seem appealing to them. The outcome of patience is reward and abundant fortune.

We must not overlook the role of Satan in this matter. His task is to kindle the fire of enmity among people and to ignite strife, so that they are diverted from what God requires. He will whisper to you: "Why be forgiving when you have been wronged? Why accept humiliation? Is he better than you?"

For since Iblis was commanded to prostrate to Adam and refused, the result was that he became cursed and expelled from the mercy of God from that moment on, and his enmity against the descendants of Adam is firmly established, and he will not leave them until he brings them to the same place he himself has come to.

Among the mercies of God toward us is that He, glory be to Him, has not left us as prey to this enemy who lies in wait for us. Rather, He has given us the protection (al-hisana) with which we fortify ourselves against him. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should come to you, then seek refuge in God⦘..﴾ [Fussilat: 36]. He reminds you of the Mighty God. If you are weak before him, then seek help against him from the Mighty God. And when he sees you in the side of God, he never dares to approach you, because you are among those whom he excepted: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad: 83].

Be aware that he will only come to you along the straight path in order to corrupt it for you. He comes to you in your prayer and reminds you of what had not been on your mind, and of the matters most important to you in this world. What matters most to him is to corrupt the Hereafter for you at any price.

So when you find in yourself something of his prodding and his whispering, say: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan." Say it in every situation in which Iblis comes to you, whether you are praying, reading the Qur'an, or engaged in any act of worship.

You may say this word without it taking you out of your worship in any way. When you persist in this word, he will despair of you and keep away from you, and he will know that you are firm and strong, drawing your strength from God. Then he will turn away from you. And why would he not, when you know his tricks and expose his schemes?

But the disappointment is that many of us follow Satan and surrender their reins to him. What Satan does with these people is give them the beginning of the thread, and leave them to unravel the rest (yukarrūn) without any effort or exertion on his part. These are the ones whom Satan has led astray and subjugated, so they walk in his train without thought or reflection.

Suppose a thief came prowling around your house, and you said, "Ahem," wanting him to hear and to know that you are awake. He will surely leave. He might think it was a coincidence and return once more, so you say, "Ahem" again. Then he knows it is not a coincidence, but that you are lying in wait for him and are alert, so he withdraws from you without return. Likewise is Satan.

We say: it is from the stupidity and heedlessness of Iblis that he announces to us his plans for misleading the children of Adam and announces his methods. Stupidity is greater for one who knows these plans and these methods, is carried along by them, and does not take precaution.

When we reflect on the words of Iblis: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and on their right and on their left⦘..﴾ [al-A'raf: 17], you notice that he left out two directions from which he did not say he would come: above and below. Why? They said: because above is the direction of turning toward God, the direction of the might of Lordship, and below represents the humility of servitude at the moment you prostrate to God in humility and submission to Him, glory be to Him. These two directions, then, Satan does not come from.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing⦘ [Fussilat: 36], nothing is hidden from His hearing. So if Satan whispers to you with speech, He hears it and knows it.

After the Qur'an has made this clarification for us, it returns to draw our attention once more to some of the signs of God in the cosmos. By these signs we infer the existence of the Creator, glory be to Him, and His power, exalted is He. Even if these signs came through the hands of scientists who disbelieve in God, we still benefit from them. Yet, alas, these scientists are wretched: they benefit all of humanity but do not benefit themselves, because, as we have said, they do not set out in their inventions and innovations from the basis of faith in the God, blessed and exalted is He. They are like beasts of burden from which people benefit by their goodness, yet nothing of that reaches them, except the fleeting enjoyment of this world.

And among the verses closest to man himself, if he reflects: for example, the normal body temperature is 37°, which you find constant in one who lives at the equator and in one who lives near the North Pole. You know the theory of thermal conduction, yet the power of God preserves this temperature for the body regardless of the surrounding climate.

Then, within the body itself, you find that the temperatures of the organs differ. The eye does not rise above 9°, while the liver performs its function only at 40°, and they are in one body and one covering, yet no conduction of heat occurs between them. This is a sign and a miracle that none but the Creator, glory be to Him, can accomplish.

Consider the blood, the fluid of life that flows within you. It must have a certain degree of fluidity within the body. If this fluidity decreases, it clots and paralysis occurs in the part where the clot forms, God forbid; and if its fluidity increases, it leads to hemorrhage. So who preserves for it this degree of fluidity? God!!

Then the Real, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And among His signs are the night and the day...﴾.

This is part 1 of 2 of the commentary of al-Sha'rawi on surah 41, verse 37.

The commentary says: "And of His signs are the night and the day..." [Fussilat: 37]. The word "min" (of) here indicates partiality. That is, these are some of God's signs in the universe. Otherwise, God's signs in His creation are numerous and countless. A sign (*ayah*) is a wondrous thing in His creation and making, which points to God's power, wisdom, and perfect craftsmanship.

"The night and the day" [Fussilat: 37] are two of God's cosmic signs. The night and the day together make up the day we know, which is the time from one sunrise to the next. God says: "He subjected them against them for seven nights and eight days in succession" [al-Haqqah: 7].

These cosmic signs mentioned here, "the night and the day, the sun and the moon" [Fussilat: 37], have taken a broad place in the procession of the messages (of the prophets) and in beliefs. In the story of our master Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he was searching for the truth and reality, he looked at the universe around him and saw a star and said: "This is my lord." But when it set, he said: "I do not love those that set." Then, when he saw the moon rising, he said: "This is my lord." But when it set, he said: "If my lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray." Then, when he saw the sun rising, he said: "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said: "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate [with God]" [al-An'am: 76–78].

So, the sun and the moon, which are linked with the night and the day, have a role in belief. This role in belief moves from the domain of belief, which is faith in the One God, to something else. This something else was made a proof of faith on a matter about which the Arabs doubted when the Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then it became a proof that revelation had not been cut off from our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

You know the story of the first revelation to the Messenger of God in the cave of Hira. He (ﷺ) would suffer and grow weary from meeting the angel, because of the difference between the angelic nature and the human nature. He (ﷺ) would go to his family saying once: "Wrap me up, wrap me up," and once: "Cover me, cover me," because of the change that was happening in his nature (ﷺ). Therefore, at the beginning, revelation was heavy upon the Messenger of God. God has said: "Indeed, We will send down upon you a heavy word" [al-Muzzammil: 5].

The companions narrated that he (ﷺ) would have sweat pouring from his forehead when the angel descended upon him. The companion who sat beside the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would lean his thigh against him, and he would feel a weight he could not bear whenever revelation descended upon the Messenger of God.

So God, glorified be He, wanted to lighten this suffering for His Messenger (ﷺ). Revelation was cut off for a period of six months, so that the Messenger of God could rest, the hardships of the first reception would leave him, and he would long to meet the angel again and to hear the speech of God, which had been cut off from him. There is no doubt that this longing would give him the strength to bear the matter of revelation and the call afterward.

The disbelievers of Mecca took the interruption of revelation from the Messenger of God as a point against him. They said: "The Lord of Muhammad has forsaken him," meaning: He has left him and abandoned him. But they did not know that the slackening of revelation is not abandonment. Rather, it is the farewell of the Beloved to His beloved, toward another meeting that is greater and longer. For this reason God, the Exalted, revealed: "By the morning brightness, and by the night when it covers with darkness. Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested [you]" [al-Duha: 1–3].

This is the point of evidence: God, glorified be He, swore to them by the morning brightness, which is the day, and by the night when it comes with its darkness. He made these two cosmic signs a proof that revelation had not been cut off. Rather, God wanted His Messenger to rest from his fatigue and to regain his vigor for receiving revelation again, just as you grow tired during the day and rest at night. "By the morning brightness, and by the night when it covers with darkness. Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested [you]" [al-Duha: 1–3]. It is well known that the morning brightness belongs to the sun and the night to the moon. Therefore, the period of the interruption of revelation to the Messenger of God is meant to lighten his burden, as He, glorified be He, says: "Did We not expand for you your breast? And We removed from you your burden, which had weighed down your back" [al-Sharh: 1–3].

The meaning is: We expanded your breast for the descent of the Qur'an upon you, so that you would long for it and have the strength to receive it. Thus the Qur'an took them from the perceptible cosmic signs to the immaterial matters, and made what they see a proof of what they deny. That is, if you, in the movement of your daily lives, need the night in which you rest and are relieved from the hardship of the day, then likewise the Messenger of God needs this period in which to rest from the hardship and weight of revelation at its beginning, so that he may renew his energy and long to meet the angel again.

For this reason, after that, He, the Exalted, said: "And the hereafter is better for you than the first" [al-Duha: 4]. So the renewal of revelation will be greater than the first and better than it, because the return will be longer and stronger.

Just as these cosmic signs, which are the night, the day, the sun, and the moon, entered into belief in the story of our master Ibrahim and into the revelation sent down to our master, the Messenger of God, likewise they entered into the resolution of some difficulties in social matters to which Islam has given attention, namely the question of equality between men and women.

This is a matter about which much debate has arisen, and those with ill intent have taken it as a pretext to attack Islam, even though Islam is the greatest religion that did justice to women, gave them their rights, and obliged society to respect them. Islam regards man and woman as two kinds of one species; that is, they are essentially one thing.

Therefore, there must be a common measure between them. When they divided into two halves, male and female, there came to be a non-common measure between them, and each of them came to have its own task in the movement of life. In order for the Qur'anic context to clarify this matter for us, He, blessed and exalted, said: "By the night when it covers, and by the day when it appears, and by Him who created the male and the female, indeed your efforts are diverse" [al-Layl: 1–4]. Just as the night and the day are complementary and cooperative, not contrary, and just as each of them has its task in life, one for work and the other for rest, so too is the case of man and woman: two elements of one thing, complementing and cooperating with each other, not opposing each other, like the night and the day. So when you look at man and woman, do not look at them as two different kinds in species that may be in conflict, for they are of one species, and one species does not clash with itself. The one species has one message; everyone cooperates in carrying it, each according to what suits them, what God created them for, and what capabilities and potentials He has given them.

This is a matter on which people have disagreed, especially the atheists, who looked at the species and did not look at what lies beneath it, male and female. Despite the difference between the two kinds, they wanted them to have one identical task with no difference between male and female.

Therefore, God, the Exalted, gives us this illustrative example: the night and the day. Is the task of the night like the task of the day? Each has its own task and nature, and whoever opposes this nature will suffer in the movement of his life. Likewise, man was made for work, strength, and striving, while woman was made for tenderness, receiving children, and raising them, especially since the childhood of a human being is the longest childhood among creatures, and overseeing it is a task of women, which men do not excel at.

So when God, glorified be He, gives us this example, He teaches us to return what we disagree about to what we agree upon. Just as we do not disagree about the task of the night and the task of the day, so too we should not disagree about the task of man and woman, and we should not repeat the word "equality" in this way without understanding the nature of each of man and woman and the role of each that God created for them.

In another place, God, glorified and exalted be He, teaches us this wisdom behind the creation of the night and the day. He says: "Say: Have you considered? If God made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you light? Will you not then listen? Say: Have you considered? If God made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you a night in which you may rest? Will you not then see?" [al-Qasas: 71–72].

After that, God, glorified and exalted be He, gave time another entrance other than the night and the day, which is the divisions of time: the hours, minutes, and seconds, by which time is regulated. The watch that sets the time for you does not perform this task unless it is itself precisely regulated. Therefore God, the Exalted, gave the sun and the moon another task, which is the task of regulating time, and so He made them precisely regulated in their movement.

He, the Exalted, says: "The sun and the moon [move] by precise reckoning" [al-Rahman: 5]; that is, by exact calculation that never differs and into which corruption never enters. From the movement of the sun and the moon we calculate time, especially religious matters, which we cannot regulate except by this movement.

He, the Exalted, said: "That you may know the number of years and the reckoning" [Yunus: 5]. From the movement of the sun I know the night and the day, and from the movement of the moon I know the beginnings and endings of the months.

So, from the movement of the sun and the moon and the night and the day, I can regulate the movement of the obligation of prayer at its various times. These times guarantee the continuous declaration of allegiance to God, the Exalted, at every time and in every place, as a result of the difference of the risings and settings throughout the complete day.

For this reason He, the Exalted, said: "Lord of the East and the West" [al-Shu'ara': 28]. In another place He said: "By the Lord of the easts and the wests" [al-Ma'arij: 40]. And He said: "Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests" [al-Rahman: 17].

Yes, there are many easts and many wests, because every place has an east and a west, and every east in one place is a west in another place, and so on. Do you not see, for example, in fasting, that we break the fast in Cairo five minutes before Alexandria? Why? Because the east of Cairo is not the east of Alexandria, and the west of Cairo is not the west of Alexandria. So we hear the announcer say: "With attention to the differences in time," that is, the time differences between one place and another.

So, the one who contemplates the movement of the sun finds that at a given moment it has a sunrise and a sunset. Accordingly, the remembrance of God in prayer and in the call to prayer flows through all of time without interruption. For this reason, the people of *tasarruf* (a term among the Sufis for the disciplined spiritual path and its practices) say: "O time, and in you is all of time." When you pray the dawn prayer, there is someone other than you praying the noon prayer, another praying the afternoon prayer, another praying the sunset prayer, and another praying the night prayer at the same time and in the same moment. So you find God, glorified be He, worshipped at every time with every kind of worship.

If you want more precision, link this matter to the second hand of your watch, not the minute or hour hand. In every second, there is a caller to prayer calling: "God is greatest." Another says: "I bear witness that there is no god but God," and another at the same moment says: "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," and so on. It is as if the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God is continuous as long as time endures and never ceases to exist.

Then God, glorified be He, gives us another observation about the sun and the moon, because they are among the greatest of creatures, and they are known for stability, precision, and grandeur in creation, to the extent that some people worshipped the sun or the moon. So God, glorified be He, wanted to draw the attention of creation to the greatness of the Creator, who is more worthy of worship than His creatures.

So He made the sun and the moon subject to a change, which is the eclipse (*kusuf*) and the lunar eclipse (*khusuf*). Whatever the sun may be, and whatever the moon may be, they are created things that change, and what changes cannot be worshipped at all. For this reason He, glorified be He, said in the verse before us: "Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to God, who created them, if it is Him you worship" [Fussilat: 37].

In the beginning of the verse God said: "And of His signs are the night and the day, the sun and the moon" [Fussilat: 37]. The verse is a wondrous thing in creation, marvelous in its order and perfection. This great creation should be glorified by God's glorification of it, but this glorification may not exceed the limit of worship, nor the limit of prostration to a created thing, however great it may be, because it is a created thing that changes, and the Deity does not change for the sake of the servants, but the servants change for the sake of God.

This matter explains to us the question of the prostration of the angels to Adam (peace be upon him). It was not a prostration of worship; rather, it was an obedience to God's command to them to prostrate to Adam. But why did God have the angels prostrate to Adam?

They said: Because Adam was going to descend to the earth, and he would have a movement of building up the earth, and the angels would be assisting him, helping him carry out his task on earth. These are the angels entrusted with the affairs of this world, those who "arrange affairs" (*al-mudabbirat amran*), as God describes them: "For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of God" [al-Ra'd: 11].

So the angels who were commanded to prostrate were not all the angels, but those who have a connection with the human being. It is as if God, glorified be He, is introducing them to this new creature, who would be in their service. So prostrate to him, a prostration of submission and obedience, so that they would know that they are in his service, arranging matters for him.

For this reason, a noble hadith has come down (in the form of continuous rotating shifts that never cease).

Among the angels there is another kind that has no connection with the human being and no relation to him. Indeed, they know nothing of this world of ours. They are the "exalted ones" (*al-'alun*) about whom God spoke regarding Iblis: "Have you become arrogant, or have you been among the exalted?" [Sad: 75].

So, if the earlier ones glorified the sun and the moon to the point of prostrating to them, then know that their Creator is more worthy of prostration: "Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to God, who created them, if it is Him you worship" [Fussilat: 37]; that is, if you are obeying His command.

We take another observation from the sun that makes us stop at something strange which we did not know before. In surah al-Kahf, the Qur'an narrates to us the journey of Dhul-Qarnayn. He, glorified be He, says: "They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: I will recite to you a mention of him. Indeed, We established him on the earth and gave him of everything a means. So he followed a way until, when he reached the setting place of the sun, he found it setting in a murky spring" [al-Kahf: 83–86].

That is, the setting place of the sun as it appears to the eye, because if you reached the murky spring, you would find the sun still far away. "And he found near it a people. We said: O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or you take among them a good way" [al-Kahf: 86], because he was a man empowered in the earth, with rank and authority.

The one empowered in the earth has the task of establishing in it the balances of justice and the standards of right and punishment, because people's movement in this world cannot be upright unless the good-doer is rewarded and the wrongdoer is punished. "He said: As for one who wrongs, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment. But as for one who believes and does righteousness, he will have the best reward, and we will speak to him of Our command with ease" [al-Kahf: 87–88].

Then he spoke of the rising of the sun, saying: ﴿Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun, he found it rising upon a people for whom We had made no screen against it﴾ [al-Kahf: 90]. That is, there is no barrier between them and it that shields it from them. He did not mention anything after the rising of the sun as he mentioned in the previous lesson concerning the setting of the sun, where he (Dhu al-Qarnayn) had a role and a course of action with those who did good and those who did evil. But regarding the rising of the sun, He said: ﴿for whom We had made no screen against it﴾ [al-Kahf: 90], and fell silent. So the purpose seems to be that we know Dhu al-Qarnayn reached a place where the day is long and nothing blocks the sun.

After scientists discovered the lines of longitude and latitude, we came to know that in some places near the poles the day lengthens until it reaches three months or six months, and this is a glimpse of the scientific miracle of the Qur'an.

If you ask: how do those who live in these places perform their prayers and fasting? We say: they estimate for the ordinary day its measure, and for the night its measure, and divide the time into night and day as is customary; and likewise for those whose night lasts three months or six months.

A final observation concerns the wording of the verse and its precise eloquence. Glorified be He, began with the sign of the night and then the day, and began with the sun and then the moon: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon...﴾ [Fussilat: 37]. The context would seem to call for saying "and the moon" to match the night, and "and the sun" to match the day.

But the wording of the Qur'an has wisdom and precise eloquence. Glorified be He begins with what is most important in the movement of life. The night was made for rest and the day for work, because the Creator, glorified be He, created man to populate the earth and to strive throughout its regions, and there is no populating except through movement, and movement requires two times: a time for rest and a time for work.

So He placed the night, the time of rest, first, because you do not produce or toil except when you have first taken your share of rest. It is as if rest first is a foundation after which work comes; otherwise the exhausted, worn-out person neither produces nor accomplishes. Likewise He placed the sun before the moon, because it is the greater and more important, and from it all the stars and planets derive their light.

Since we are discussing the night and the day, this question must confront us: which of them came first in creation? Some say: the night first, on the evidence that we establish, for example, the entry of Ramadan by its night, not its day: when we see the crescent we say, "Tomorrow is Ramadan." Those who believe that the night existed first must have another premise, namely that the day did not precede the night.

Glorified be He settles this matter, saying: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each is travelling in an orbit﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40].

We thus arrive at a cosmic reality which He, glorified be He, has affirmed: neither does the day precede the night, nor does the night precede the day, because, as we have explained, they both came into existence together at the beginning of creation, at one and the same time, and then each revolved with the other.

Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But if they are arrogant...﴾ [Fussilat: 38], meaning: if they turn away from obeying Allah in His command and prohibition in the verse before it: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them...﴾ [Fussilat: 37]. Arrogance here indicates a lack of faith in Allah, the One who commands and forbids, because they prostrated to the sun and prostrated to the moon in worship, and worship means the worshipper's obedience to the command of the one worshipped. The sun and the moon have no commands and no prohibitions, so their worship is invalid, and it shows the foolishness of whoever worships them and the falsehood of this worship, because they are creatures with no command, no prohibition, and no obligations. They do not reward those who obey them, and they do not punish those who disobey them.

Therefore we say: the word "worship" here is false and baseless (fanṭaziyyah), meaning: what matters is that they have an object of worship that satisfies their desire for religiosity, and how easy it is for a person to take as an object of worship something that has no obligations.

Therefore, when they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to Allah in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], we say: the word "worship them" here is false, as evidence that when harm befalls you, you do not turn to the sun or the moon, but turn to Allah: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon disappear except Him...﴾ [al-Isra': 67].

And He said: ﴿And when harm touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning back to Him...﴾ [al-Rum: 33].

And the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But if they are arrogant, those who are with your Lord glorify Him by night and by day, and they never tire﴾ [Fussilat: 38].

The meaning: Allah, glorified is He, is free of need for the obedience of these arrogant ones and of their worshippers. He has noble angels who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and who do what they are commanded. They glorify Him night and day without ceasing, and they have no work except glorification, and they do not tire, grow weary, or become exhausted.

They said regarding the "with-ness" here, ﴿those who are with your Lord﴾ [Fussilat: 38], that it is a with-ness of rank, not of place, a with-ness of honour and nobility, as He, glorified is He, said about the martyrs: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 169].

And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and rivers, in a seat of truth, near a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 54-55].

So these angels are not in one place with Allah, nor do they sit with Him, glorified is He; rather, they are exactly like us: they do not see Allah, and they believe in Him as we do, in the unseen, and Allah is unseen to them. Some interpretations, and I favour them, incline to the view that Allah, the Exalted, has no place, because He is in every place, so every place is "with Allah."

For this reason, read the words of the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you at that time are looking on — and We are closer to it than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 83-85]. Some say: the "with-ness" here is a with-ness of knowledge; but if it were so, He would not have said ﴿but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 85]. Since He said ﴿but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 85], it is a true with-ness, pervasive in every place.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 41, verse 39:

The Qur'anic context continues to lead us to the cosmic signs that establish the power of the Creator, glory be to Him. ﴿And among His signs...﴾ Here we have said it is partitive (tab'id). That is: these are some of the signs of God (His signs), i.e., the cosmic ones that point to His power, exalted be He, and they are the wondrous things that indicate the excellence of the craftsmanship. ﴿That you see the earth humbled...﴾ That is: still and at rest, with nothing upon it of crops, for example, because the earth was created to be a soil for plants. It is as if the earth on which there is no crop is a sorrowful, humbled, silent and motionless earth, because it has not brought forth growth, and perhaps in this it resembles the woman who does not bear children.

﴿But when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells.﴾ "Stirs" (ihtazzat): moves. "Swells" (wa rabat): increases and expands. You see the sprouting broad bean, for example, is dry and rigid; when you wet it with water, it increases in size and expands. What is meant is: it stirs and moves with what grows out of it of plants.

﴿Indeed, He who revives it...﴾ That is: He who revived this still earth with vegetation and transformed it into this fresh green carpet ﴿is certainly the Giver of life to the dead.﴾ So then: take from this sensory, observed verse a proof for the truth of what is hidden from you and what God has told you about the matter of the resurrection of the dead. O you who deny the resurrection and the revival of the dead, is there not for you a lesson in the reviving of the barren, parched earth with vegetation?

﴿Indeed, He is Able to do all things.﴾ That is: the power of God in it is absolute, because nothing can overpower Him, glory be to Him, and He who created the first creation from nothing is more capable of restoring it...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 41, verse 40:

His saying, may He be exalted: "yulhidun" (يُلْحِدُونَ). That is: they incline the signs of Allah away from truth and uprightness toward falsehood which they themselves regard as truth, or they distort the signs in accordance with their desires, because the signs of Allah have meanings, and so they commit ilhad (deviation, distortion) concerning them. That is: they conceal them and display other false meanings for them, just as we bury the dead in the depths of the earth after he used to walk upon it. The meaning is that they hide their realities in order to satisfy their disbelief and their desires.

Among the ilhad concerning the signs of Allah is what some have fallen into of tashbih (likening) or tamthil (equating) in the names and attributes of Allah. When they stop at an attribute of Allah that has a counterpart among human beings, they liken Him. Allah has hearing that is not like our hearing, a hand that is not like our hands, and sight that is not like our sight. Therefore, we must take these attributes within the general framework of the decisive verses: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11].

Among it is their saying about the miracle that it is sihr (sorcery), in the story of Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) with Pharaoh, and the difference between sorcery and miracle: the miracle is a reality, while sorcery is imagination far from reality. It is true that the miracle of Musa (peace be upon him) was of the same kind as sorcery, because it was the field in which his people excelled, but it was not sorcery.

The ropes which the sorcerers of Pharaoh threw, Musa saw as serpents moving swiftly, while the sorcerers themselves saw them as ropes. Sorcery makes you imagine a thing to be other than it is, though in reality it is not so; it is merely imagination. Therefore Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿It was imagined to him, by their sorcery, that their ropes were moving swiftly﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66]. Imagination, not reality...

Just as they said that Musa (peace be upon him) was a sorcerer, they said it of Sayyidna Muhammad (ﷺ), and the refutation of it, as we have explained, is simple. We say to them: if Muhammad were a sorcerer, he would have bewitched those who believed in him, so why did he not bewitch you as well, and the matter would end?

Among their ilhad concerning the signs of Allah is their saying about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he is majnun (mad), although they never tested him in anything of that sort. He was known among them as "the Truthful, the Trustworthy," and he was characterized among them by noble character, and one of noble character can never be mad. Allah has answered them: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2].

Among their ilhad regarding the Qur'an is that they said it is poetry (shi'r). It is strange of them to say so, because they are the most knowledgeable of people regarding the methods of poets and the expressions of poets. They know that the Qur'an is miraculous, that it is from Allah, that its style cannot be matched, and that it is unique of its kind, yet they lie. This is ilhad...

Among their ilhad is that they change what is required of them and distort words. Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words from their places and say, "We hear and we disobey," and "Hear without being made to hear," and "Ra'ina," twisting with their tongues and defaming the religion﴾ [an-Nisa: 46]...

So the aspects of their ilhad concerning the signs of Allah are many. Allah has informed us that they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of; what they did not forget, they distorted; and what they did not distort, they concealed. Would that they had stopped at this limit, but their audacity against Allah reached the point of writing the Book with their own hands and saying: "This is from Allah," when it is not from Allah. All of this is different forms of their ilhad.

Therefore, the Truth, glorified be He, informs here: ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our signs are not hidden from Us﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. Yes, they are not hidden from the knowledge of Allah, so the fact that they are not hidden is a necessary matter; but the purpose is that we inform them of their crime so that we may punish them for it, because the crime is one thing and the punishment for it is another. The Truth makes them aware of their crime so that there may be a basis for the punishment, as the people of law say: "There is no crime except by text." It is as if the Truth, glorified be He, does not seize them unawares, nor leave them in blindness, but makes things clear to them before He calls them to account.

﴿Then is he who is thrown into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ This is a question whose answer is known, and the Truth asks us while He knows the answer will be as He wills, glorified be He. It is as if the Truth, glorified be He, says to us through this question: be eager to carry out the commands of Allah, and beware of the prohibitions, so avoid them. This is the path of security and salvation from the Fire. Is he who is thrown into the Fire equal to he who comes secure and safe?

Since this question comes after the discussion of ilhad concerning the signs of Allah, the meaning becomes: those who deviate concerning the signs of Allah will be cast into the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and those who do not deviate concerning the signs of Allah will come secure.

It is foolish for a person to deviate concerning the signs of Allah in order to obtain temporal authority or a temporary status, whose end is certain extinction, and then to meet after that a painful destiny in an eternal Fire that has no end.

Come to the greatest of people in bliss in this life, who has taken from it wealth, strength, authority, awe, and all glory, and ask him: does anything spoil this blessing? He will tell you: "I fear that it will not last." Yes, the impermanence of it spoils it for its possessors: either the blessing leaves them while they are alive and provided for, or they leave it by death.

Therefore, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informs us of the state of these pampered disbelievers in this world: how are they in the Hereafter? The Messenger says: "One of them will be dipped once into the Fire, may Allah protect us, then the angels will ask him: 'Did you ever see any bliss in the world?' He will say: 'No, by Allah, I never saw any bliss at all!'"

So who would leave an everlasting, enduring blessing for a spoiled, passing, perishable blessing? Then you enjoy yourself in this world according to your capacities and abilities, while in the Hereafter you will enjoy according to the power, generosity and bounty of Allah, in a Garden containing what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

Since we are before two matters that are not equal, and the right course in them is clear, and since we have made this clarification for you, you are free; choose for yourselves: ﴿Do what you will; indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ The imperative here is for threat and warning. That is: do what you wish, for Allah sees you, Allah is aware of your deeds, and He is able to recompense you for them with a fitting recompense.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 41, verse 41:

Kufr (disbelief) here is used in the sense of concealment, meaning: the concealing of faith in the necessary existence (of God). For concealment requires something concealed, so what is the thing concealed in the process of disbelief? Disbelief conceals its opposite; it conceals faith. So it is as if faith is an innate matter (fitri), and it is the origin, while disbelief is something that has come upon it in order to cover it. And it is as if disbelief in this sense is a soldier from among the soldiers of faith and a proof of it.

As for the word bil-dhikr (﴿بِالذِّكْرِ﴾), here it means the Qur'an, which was sent down upon the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)...

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وَإِنَّهُ لَكِتَابٌ عَزِيزٌ﴾ ("And indeed it is a Book of might"), the word 'aziz (عزيز) has several meanings, among them: 'aziz, meaning rare and precious; and 'aziz, meaning the dominant, the one who cannot be overcome. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَاللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ ذُو انْتِقَامٍ﴾ [Al-Imran: 4] ("And Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution"). So the Qur'an is dominant, it rises and nothing rises above it; it takes hold of hearts and overpowers them, as evidenced by their saying: ﴿لاَ تَسْمَعُواْ لِهَـٰذَا الْقُرْآنِ وَالْغَوْاْ فِيهِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَغْلِبُونَ﴾ [Fussilat: 26] ("Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you will overcome").

That is because whoever hears the words of the Qur'an must be struck with awe by it, provided that he receives it with a pure heart and a non-rigid conscience...

The disbelief (kufr) here means concealment (satr), i.e., concealing faith in the existence of the Necessary Being (wajib al-wujud), because concealment requires something concealed. So what is the thing concealed in the act of disbelief? Disbelief conceals its opposite, faith. It is as if faith is the innate natural disposition (fitrah) and the original state, while disbelief is an accidental addition laid over it to cover it. In this sense, disbelief is like a soldier among the soldiers of faith and an evidence for it.

The word ﴿بِٱلذِّكْرِ..﴾ [Fussilat: 41] here means the Qur'an that was sent down upon the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. The term dhikr is also applied to the scriptures that preceded the Qur'an: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43].

And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48]. Dhikr is also used to mean reputation and standing. ﴿And indeed, it [the Qur'an] is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44], meaning the Qur'an. And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10].

Dhikr is also applied to the glorification of Allah: ﴿Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91].

Dhikr is also applied to remembrance of Allah through obedience, and to Allah's remembrance of the servant through bounties and forgiveness: ﴿So remember Me; I will remember you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152].

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, it is a Book of might﴾ [Fussilat: 41], the word 'azIz has several meanings. Among them: 'azIz meaning rare and precious, and 'azIz meaning the Overpowering, which cannot be overcome. From this is His saying: ﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4]. So the Qur'an is overpowering; it rises and nothing rises above it. It seizes hearts and takes possession of them, as evidenced by their saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and speak noisily during it that you may overcome﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

That is because whoever hears the words of the Qur'an must be astonished by it, on condition that he receives it with a pure heart and a living conscience, not a rigid one. If it meets good reception, it has this effect which we saw in the story of the Islam of our master 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). He was among the fiercest enemies of Islam until the moment he learned of the Islam of his sister and her husband. He came to her and slapped her until blood flowed from her face. This blood became the cause of the softening of his heart, a softening that overcame his ignorance. So when he heard the Qur'an from her this time, he heard it with a heart, emotions and a pure sentiment, and he was affected by it and embraced Islam.

Therefore: the Qur'an is mighty and overpowering. For this reason, it is reported in the noble hadith that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [...] And: when you want to choose between two matters or weigh them against each other, you must be completely clear of mind and bring out of your heart any desire for either of them, then weigh them, and whatever you find comfort in, proceed with it. For this reason Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his body﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4].

Therefore: it is one heart. If it is filled with evil, how can it receive good? You must first expel the evil, because evil will drive out good.

Allah the Exalted says about the reception of the Qur'an by the hypocrites and disbelievers: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until, when they leave you, they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he just say?"﴾ [Muhammad: 16]. That is: as if they were not affected by it and did not understand it, out of arrogance and obstinacy. Allah responded to them: ﴿Say, "It is for those who believe a guidance and healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is for them blindness"﴾ [Fussilat: 44], i.e., the Qur'an.

So the Qur'an is one, but its effect differs according to the recipient. It is guidance and healing for the people of faith, and blindness for the people of disbelief and hypocrisy.

Therefore: the Truthful, glorified is He, wants from us justice in choosing, justice in seeking, and justice in weighing the two matters. If this justice is present, then the Qur'an will inevitably prevail. Nothing contests or competes with the Qur'an when it is received properly. Even in matters where the intellect stands still, you find the conscience affirming them.

Therefore we have said: the inspiration of the Merciful is not chased away by the inspiration of Satan. Did the inspiration of the Merciful oppose the mother of Moses when He said to her: ﴿And when you fear for him, then cast him into the river and do not fear or grieve﴾ [al-Qasas: 7]? The intellect does not accept this, but the pure conscience accepts it. Those who heard the Qur'an and were not affected by it, and it did not bear its fruit in their souls, merely listened while preoccupied with its opposite.

So we are in need of justice in choosing, then protection of the choice. Therefore, in response to whoever claims that Islam was spread by the sword, we say: this is not correct. The sword in the history of Islam did not come to impose a creed; it came to protect choice, and to protect the freedom of religion to declare itself. Freedom of belief is something Islam guaranteed, as evidenced by the fact that it left in Muslim lands people upon their disbelief and their religions, and He said: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

Because Islam proceeded from freedom of belief and made religion a matter of choice, it ruled that the apostate be killed. Strangely, the enemies of Islam take this matter as a criticism of the religion of Allah, saying: Islam fights freedom of belief and compels people to embrace it.

This is a false accusation. The one who reflects finds that Islam announces this ruling to whoever has not yet believed. It says to him: Be mindful before you enter Islam, and note that you will be killed if you apostatize from it. This is an obstacle on the path of Islam that tests its adherents, so that none comes to it except one who has been convinced by it and Islam has settled in his heart without dispute. The ruling to kill the apostate protects your turning to it as a choice and alerts you: either you turn away, or you recognize that it is the truth and believe in it.

As for His saying: ﴿No falsehood can approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42], it means that falsehood cannot reach it from any direction. Therefore the orientalists have tried to find a flaw in the Qur'an... but far from it for them. They stopped, for example, at His saying: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and in another place He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for them and for you﴾ [al-Isra': 31].

They saw repetition in the two verses and said: if the Qur'an is eloquent, which of the two verses is more eloquent? And if one of them is eloquent, the other is not. These people lack the faculty that helps them understand the words of Allah and receive His guidance. Had they looked at the context, they would have found that the two verses differ in subject matter, so there is no repetition, and each is eloquent in expressing its subject.

As for His saying: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for you and for them﴾ [al-An'am: 151], it is as if poverty already exists for the one addressed; he is preoccupied first with providing for himself before being preoccupied with providing for his children. Therefore the verse concludes with His saying: ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾ [al-An'am: 151]. In the other, He says ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra': 31], meaning poverty does not yet exist but he fears it when a child comes. So Allah reassured him that the child will come with its provision, and said: ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾ [al-Isra': 31]. Thus each verse is eloquent in its place.

Likewise they stopped at His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, and no compensation will be accepted from it, and no intercession will benefit it, and they will not be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], and in the other verse: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, and no compensation will be accepted from it, and no intercession will benefit it, and they will not be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123].

The hasty glance sees no difference between the two verses, but the one who reflects and has linguistic faculty notices the difference. The two verses speak of two souls: a soul that recompenses and a soul for which recompense is made. The soul for which recompense is made acknowledges its sin and says: take justice and leave me. We say to it: No. So it goes to someone greater than itself to intercede for it. Thus justice is presented first, and when it does not benefit it, intercession is presented.

As for the recompensing soul, which is the intercessor, when it first stands before Allah the Exalted it says: O Lord, I intercede for so-and-so. If his intercession is not accepted, then take justice from me. Thus each verse is eloquent in its place. But what shall we do with those who do not understand from Allah and do not receive well, yet accuse the words of Allah?! They say: Your Lord said such-and-such. Yes, He is our Lord, praise be to Allah, and we would love for your Lord to be ours too.

Among the verses they stopped at is His saying: ﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah will perfect His light, although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ [al-Saff: 8]. They say: where is the dominance of Islam over all religions, when after fourteen centuries there still exist in the world Jews, atheists, Christians, and other religions? This statement also shows their failure to understand the expression and meanings of the Noble Qur'an.

The meaning of ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Saff: 9] does not mean that all people become Muslims, because the meaning of prevalence here is the prevalence of proof, i.e., He declares His strong proof. After that, they have freedom: whoever believes believes, and whoever disbelieves disbelieves. That is another subject.

Had you been reading the Qur'an with insight, you would know that the prevalence of Islam over other religions will occur alongside the continuation of polytheism and disbelief, as evidenced by the wording of the verse. Once He said: ﴿although the polytheists dislike it﴾ [al-Saff: 9], and once: ﴿although the disbelievers dislike it﴾ [al-Saff: 8].

Thus both exist alongside Islam. It suffices for Islam's prevalence over other religions that they are compelled to adopt its rulings and judgments while not being Muslims, and their life circumstances force them to find no solution except in Islam. This is the greatness of prevalence.

You know that the Vatican opposed the issue of divorce which Islam brought, but over time and with the multiplication of their problems, they were compelled to act upon it as a solution to their problems. They adopted the ruling of Islam while not being Muslims.

Therefore: Allah has spoken the truth: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisa': 82]. These verses and others guide us to the soundness of the words of Allah and their freedom from falsehood and contradiction. ﴿No falsehood can approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42], because falsehood only comes when the speaker is not right, and who speaks the Qur'an? Allah.

Therefore He said after it: ﴿A revelation from the All-Wise, Praiseworthy﴾ [Fussilat: 42]. "Hakim" and "hamid" are intensive forms (sigha al-mubalagha) from wisdom and praise. Wisdom requires placing a thing in its appropriate position, and praise means that He, the Exalted, is praised for all His actions, all His decrees, and all His destinies. Thus "al-hamdu lillah" is connected from beginning to end.

Therefore we have said regarding His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2] that among His mercies toward us is that He taught us the formula of His praise for His blessings. He brought it in the form of the subject and predicate (al-hamdu lillah), because if He had not set for His servants a formula of praise for Him, the servants would have differed about it, people would have varied in it, and an eloquent man of letters would have had a praise that the unlettered person and the shepherd could not match.

Had this matter been left to people's abilities, there would have been no equality of opportunity in praising Allah. Thus among His mercy to us is that He said: raise your hands from composing the formula, and I have set it for you, so that all My creation may equally share in praising Me and glorifying Me. Everyone says one word, (al-hamdu lillah) only, and I want nothing more from you than that.

Therefore our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), taught us to say in praise of Allah: "Subhanaka la nuhsi thana'an 'alayka anta kama athnayta 'ala nafsik" (Glory be to You, we cannot count the praise upon You; You are as You have praised Yourself). Whoever has learned this formula (al-hamdu lillah) and has been guided to say it should praise Allah for it itself, praising Allah for teaching him how to praise Him. Thus the praise of the servant to Allah remains connected, and the servant remains praising his Lord with a praise that has no end.

When you hear the word ﴿tanzil﴾ [Fussilat: 42], you feel that it is sent down from above, even if what is sent down is of earthly material, as in His saying in Surat al-Hadid: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great military strength and benefits for the people﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. Though iron is in the earth, it is sent down from the height of the creating power to serve the servants on earth.

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, consoles His Messenger (ﷺ) and lightens for him what he encounters of the harm and obstinacy of the polytheists, saying, exalted is He:

﴿Nothing is said to you except...﴾.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi), surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66, on surah 41, verse 43:

It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): O Muhammad, you are the master of the messengers, and the messengers were harmed. Had harm been in proportion to rank, the harm your people inflict upon you would be many times the harm inflicted upon the earlier messengers. Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you, so you are no novelty among the messengers.

What was said to the messengers before you is: ﴿And
 indeed Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed they would be the ones helped, and indeed Our soldiers would be the victors.﴾ [al-Saffat: 171-173]. You, O Muhammad, are one of them, so rejoice in God's victory for you, for your soldiers, and for those who follow you.

It is also valid that the meaning of ﴿Nothing is said to you﴾ [Fussilat: 43] is: from your enemies and those who oppose you, and ﴿except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ [Fussilat: 43] is: from their enemies and those who opposed them. The meaning is: do not grieve, for this is God's way with the people of callings and the bearers of messages. You are one of them, so do not wear yourself out, and do not burden yourself in the cause of your call with what you cannot bear.

﴿So whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you in death, to Us they will be returned.﴾ [Ghafir: 77]

That is because our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he tasted the sweetness of faith in God, loved all people. He had a zeal for his Lord, wanting all people to submit, so that none of them would escape and none would deviate from faith in God. Therefore he exerted himself greatly, and his Lord often rebuked him for this, with the rebuke of a lover to his beloved: ﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself with grief over them, if they do not believe in this message.﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]

And He made clear to him (ﷺ): ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the conveyance [of the message].﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 18]

We often see the Noble Qur'an narrating to our master, the Messenger of God, the stories of the earlier prophets, as consolation for the Messenger of God and as lightening his burden... And His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Forgiving and has painful punishment.﴾ Reflect on this statement, which the scholars call targhib wa tarhib (encouragement and warning). The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, takes into account the conditions of these opponents of His Messenger (ﷺ), and addresses them in a way that suits every possibility. Whoever of them returns to the truth and to the straight path, the door of repentance is open, and God is Forgiving and Merciful. Whoever persists and continues in his opposition, God is the possessor of painful punishment.

You notice here that forgiveness precedes punishment. Indeed, the Truth, glory be to Him, promises whoever believes and whose faith is good that He will expiate his sins and increase him by changing his evil deeds into good deeds, out of grace and generosity. It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is making His servants feel close and drawing their hearts toward Him, though He is free of need of them.

The history of Islam is full of those who clashed with Islam and its call, who opposed the Messenger of God and the believers with him, and who were the fiercest enemies, but afterward became bearers of its banner and offered their souls cheaply in its cause. Had the door been closed in their faces, they would not have entered the religion of God. You know the story of the conversion of 'Umar, Hamza, 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Khalid, 'Amr, and others who were the chieftains of disbelief.
